subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY IMPROVED EXPORT MARKETS WILL PRODUCE ENOUGH JOBS TO TAKE CARE OF INCREASED LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Since the drop in export production as a proportion of our total production between 1973 and 1975 was only about 2 per cent, and since in his budget address of last Wednesday the minister based his job forecast figures on a recovery in the export market, I ask, does he think that even if the 2 per cent drop which took place between 1973 and 1975 is fully restored it will be sufficient to produce enough jobs in the Canadian economy next year?

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY IMPROVED EXPORT MARKETS WILL PRODUCE ENOUGH JOBS TO TAKE CARE OF INCREASED LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, although I do not have the actual text of the speech before me, my recollection is that we estimated that the export drop last year was at a rate of 7 per cent. Of course, that is in the budget text. The recovery on the export side will be a major factor in creating increased employment in Canada, which will in due course enable the economy to provide jobs for the substantial numbers of people, particularly young people, coming into the labour force.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY IMPROVED EXPORT MARKETS WILL PRODUCE ENOUGH JOBS TO TAKE CARE OF INCREASED LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Since it is forecast that 250,000 new jobs will be created next year, which is about 100,000 less than the anticipated increase in the numbers of people coming on the job market, is it the minister's view that, even if the international economy recovers as fully as he seems to anticipate, as an absolute minimum during the coming year Canadians can expect an increase of 100,000 in the numbers of the unemployed?

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY IMPROVED EXPORT MARKETS WILL PRODUCE ENOUGH JOBS TO TAKE CARE OF INCREASED LABOUR FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the estimate is that there would not be that additional number of people coming into the work force. The estimates indicate a rough balance, which is one reason why we did not anticipate during the current year, at least, being able to take the level of unemployment substantially below the levels we have been incurring in the last six to eight months.

Is he saying that next year he anticipates only 250,000 more people coming into the labour force? Is that the anticipated increase in the labour force? In conclusion, has the minister estimated where the new jobs are to be created? If, in the main, they depend on improvements in our export business, does it mean that most of them will be

created in central Canada? Or can the Atlantic provinces, which will be badly hit by the Unemployment Insurance Act changes, anticipate an increased share in the numbers of new jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: AREA IN WHICH NEW JOBS MIGHT BE CREATED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is useful nor particularly helpful to try to break down into small figures or divisions what is, after all, an estimate only. subsubtopic: BEQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF SLOW ANSWERS TO APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
At a time when most Canadian citizens feel that unemployment is growing a little too fast, projects are presented to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and there are complaints that it takes an extremely long time before these applications from citizens throughout Canada are answered. Could the minister indicate to the House why it takes so long before reaching a decision which could mean work for many unemployed people in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lessard (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: BEQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF SLOW ANSWERS TO APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say to the hon. member that the offers of monetary assistance to industries are issued every week by the department, and I believe the hon. member has been able to realize that there is a substantial number of projects processed each week by the department.
But in reply to the specific question of the hon. member, I would like to say that the department endeavours to reach a decision, make an offer or reject the application within a period of 90 days. That is our objective. Unfortunately this period starts to run from the time when the applicant has supplied us with all the information related to his or her project. Most applications, when received, do not include all the elements required to allow our analysts to assess it and reach a decision. They have to contact the applicant several times and that explains in most cases the long delays before a decision is made.
Of course, there are also exceptional, complex and difficult cases where we have to conduct a detailed analysis, check throughout the country for the types of businesses that exist in the same field, the degree of competition, and to what extent the market is already supplied by Canadian
Oral Questions
producers. For all these reasons, we do need a certain period of time.

subsubtopic: BEQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF SLOW ANSWERS TO APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. I thank the minister for the elaborate explanations he has just provided me about it being necessary to have 90 days to make a decision. subsubtopic: BEQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF SLOW ANSWERS TO APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to add this. Fairly frequently, our civil servants go on the site but you will understand that it is difficult to do this in every case. But you will understand, Mr. Speaker, that despite all the diligence we can ask from our civil servants, it remains that some applications are difficult to process because of specific projects. subsubtopic: STUDY INDICATING RUSTING OF VEHICLES SAFETY HAZARD-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Transport. Last week, officials of his department said that after a five months study carried out both in England and in Canada, it was clear that even a small degree of rust in motor vehicles produced a serious driving hazard. The same officials said that neither the minister nor the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs would take these findings seriously. So, I ask the minister why is it that neither he nor his colleague the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will give credence to these findings and take action on behalf of Canadian consumers? Will the minister assure the House that the findings of the Motor Vehicle Safety Branch will be made public for the benefit of Canadian consumers and that immediate action will be taken?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STUDY INDICATING RUSTING OF VEHICLES SAFETY HAZARD-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
The main reason for not taking those findings seriously was that those were not the findings. There were reports of a study by someone who was attached either to a department or to an agency but the view of the department is that while rusting is obviously a serious matter in terms of the economics of motor vehicles it is not a safety hazard. Our department has been carrying out tests on vehicles rusted to various stages and has found there is no significant

additional safety problem. Naturally, if the rust has caused defects which are noticeable that is another issue, but in terms of the rust itself as a safety hazard, apart from the economics, it is not such a hazard as the hon. member implies.

speechtext: A supplementary question. I also mentioned the British findings which were made in conjunction with the Canadian findings according to which a serious safety hazard was evident. In view of those findings I ask the minister whether legislation will be introduced which would require vehicle manufacturers to rustproof parts before they are assembled. I would also ask the minister whether he would outline to the House the current status of his negotiations with the Ford Motor Company of Canada regarding the rusting problems which affect thousands of Canadian consumers today.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STUDY INDICATING RUSTING OF VEHICLES SAFETY HAZARD-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: The studies on which the hon. member is relying, including those referring to other countries, amounted only to an examination of some literature on the subject setting out someone's theory of what might happen as a result of rusting. On the other hand we are performing actual tests and it is upon this evidence that we are relying.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Minister of Transport. speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: FREIGHT RATES-REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON PROPOSED CHANGE IN RATES ON RAPESEED PRODUCTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the problem in respect of rapeseed crushing plants really emerged when very high competitive conditions began to exist in the oil industry and they were faced with an existing discrepancy between the low rate on rapeseed and a much higher rate on rapeseed oil. Our recent disposition of the appeal has not raised the rate as such, but has ordered the CTC not to allow rates to be charged higher than compensatory. This will, for instance, lead to a lower rate than the one faced by the Lloydminster plant. It may have a marginal effect on the rate on rapeseed to other plants. Really the problem relates to the long existing differential between the low rate on rapeseed and the higher rate on rapeseed oil. In fact, no change has taken place in the rates. The direction from us was simply not to allow a rate higher than compensatory, and so far no change in rates has been filed. I do not know how many months it will be before the actual filing and assessing of that rate will take place. It quite likely will be after the Snavely Commission has reported in any case.

Second, on December 2, 1975, when a telex was sent to Lockheed confirming the government's intention to purchase 18 "Orion" aircraft, neither myself nor my deputy minister was made aware, directly or indirectly, of a telephone conversation held between an official of the Department of National Defence and a representative of Lockheed to the effect that Lockheed would furnish the financing for the LRPA project. In any case, I repeat that not obtaining a written agreement from Lockheed was a serious error. It is elementary that an agreement involving a loan of millions of dollars should have been confirmed in a written document. This was not done. Furthermore, the offer never did materialize. In this respect, I refer to the statements of my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, which appear in Hansard dated March 30, 1976, on page 12265 and March 26, 1976, page 12177.

During the past months I have repeatedly attempted to ascertain whether or not any officials of my department were aware of the financing negotiations held between DND and Lockheed prior to December 2, 1975. I repeatedly was assured that no one had prior knowledge of this problem, and I conveyed this information to the House. On May 19, in view of the numerous questions raised by members in the House, I personally met, in the presence of my deputy minister, Mr. L. H. Stopforth, who assured me that he had no prior information concerning the financial negotiations between DND and Lockheed. Ministers, acting on the representations and advice of their civil servants, must rely on the information they receive on these matters on the basis of trust. Last evening, however-and it was confirmed to me this morning-I learned that Mr. L. H. Stopforth had modified his version to state that, while he had not been privy to conversations between DND and Lockheed, he was aware of the financing discussions with Lockheed in November, 1975.
I take my ministerial responsibilities very seriously with regard to the policies and administrative practices of my department. Accordingly, I will stand by my officials and I
June 1, 1976

accept responsibility for errors of judgment, mistakes made in good faith and inadvertent errors. But I do not believe that ministerial responsibility extends to cases of misinformation or gross negligence. In this case, a serious error was committed. Not only were I and my deputy minister not informed of financial negotiations between DND and Lockheed prior to December 2, but subsequently, when I personally checked on this situation, I remained misinformed. This is unacceptable. My view is that while ministerial responsibility is of prime importance, every public servant, regardless of his interest in politics, also holds the public trust to some extent. Every public servant is in a position of responsibility, and the responsibility here was to ensure that the minister, the House and the public were correctly informed.
I feel very strongly about officials who misinform their minister. While I am not against any man or any organization, I believe that preserving the integrity and the efficiency of our system of government comes first. The public must believe that the system serves it well. The public must respect the public service. The public has a right to be accurately informed. My ministerial responsibility in this case is to see that these rights are preserved. Consequently, Mr. L. H. Stopforth has been removed from his functions as deputy head of the project office.

It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that if we go back over the history of Canadian Parliament and if we look at what we are doing today, we must unfortunately recognize that at the present time, what the hon. minister of Supply and

Services (Mr. Goyer) stated in this House and the development of the long term policy of former governments and the present administration aims simply at placing the administration of the federal government in the hands of people who were not elected for this purpose.

I think that it is too easy to blame a public servant for a mistake which was made by the government. Yet, two ministers and two departments are involved in the Lockheed affair, and today, the minister of Supply and Services thinks that he will get out of it simply by transferring, by removing- perhaps with a future promotion; in any case, we shall see later-by transferring a senior public servant who is now accused of having been the cause of this serious mistake by the government, without making a further investigation to find out who are the true culprits, when the government seemed well aware of what was going on in the two departments concerned and when the minister tells this House that because of erroneous information on the part of the department, the government, which means the Canadian taxpayer, will now have to pay this mistake between $16 million and $30 million.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to summarize my thinking before getting into a more detailed explanation by quoting part of an editorial published in the Vancouver Sun of January 18, 1975. This article is entitled:
How powerful mandarins confiscated from members of parliament-
-and we could add "from the ministers"-
-the right to legislate
The truth, not easily admitted by the members in the opposition as well as those in the government, is that more often than not the senior officials are those who are running, sometimes interpreting the legislation according to their views and at times in having passed the legislation they see fit.
The Committee on Statutory Instruments has been set up following a 1969 committee report, whose conclusion surprised no one in the capital, that a large part of our laws do not emanate from legislators but from bureaucrats.
Parliament alone may pass legislation but those acts are so general that for the average citizen the noble intention of the elected representatives are often less important than the restrictive regulations laid down by the bureaucrats after the legislation has been passed.
Today, bureaucrats have by law the authority to lay down regulations.
Regulations appear less redoubtable than legislation, but the difference is more in words than in reality. A lot of regulations have force of law because they can be enforced by the court and officers, much like all regulations passed by the House.
The McCleave committee which had a small group of law students at its disposal received no fewer than 1,900 delegated legislative measures, that is regulations which were drafted by people who rule but were not elected and which were applicable in 1972, 1973 and 1974. That is the pace at which bureaucracy is passing legislation and that pace has not slowed down since the survey made in 1969 by the McGuigan committee, the hon. member for Windsor-Walk-erville. The committee found that from 1956 to 1968, 6,992 regulations were published in the Canada Gazette covering
June 1, 1976

19,972 pages, and most of them have force of law. Moses was satisfied with ten commandments but that time is over and it is quite different today.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) said it is a fact that the many laws governing us are not promulgated by Parliament but scores of departments and organizations which were given the necessary power. Echoing the committee, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said that the increasing threat posed by statutory instruments, decrees and orders in council are a plague that affects most democracies. The Liberal member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) stated that the overflowing activity of the government can have the dangerous effect of bringing specialized senior public servants to run the people they are supposed to serve.
Mr. Speaker, today members of Parliament serve public servants and yet members of Parliament were elected to serve their voters. We are living in a democracy where bureaucracy makes up democracy. Mr. Speaker, a little further one could read:
The committee proposes to demand that every legislation emanating from senior public servants be presented to Parliament so members will discuss it openly before it is implemented.
This article was written many years ago, Mr. Speaker.

In certain cases indeed, in nearly any constituency be it represented by a Liberal, a Conservative or a Social Crediter, constituents come up and ask their M.P.'s help to settle a problem they cannot solve in matters of unemployment insurance for example, of welfare or that sort of things. When those constituents call at a government office saying that they have consulted with their member of Parliament, they are immediately snubbed and told there is no use to consult with a member, because members account for nothing, nobody needs them and they have no business coming up and telling public servants what to do in government offices. Mr. Speaker, I will relate something which happened to us, the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada, in 1974. We had passed a legislation here in August-
That does not happen only to you!

The legislation-yes, yes; that happens to you too!
June 1, 1976

Mr. Speaker, the Canada Elections Act clearly provides that any political party has the right to receive donations and to issue receipts for these gifts in favour of their electoral organization. The act provides that rendered services may be included. This means that the travel expenses of a constituent or party worker who goes from one riding to another or anywhere in Canada can be figured out and deducted on one's income return as political contributions, under the electoral legislation passed by Parliament. That is what we did under the terms of the act.
But the bureaucrats the Department of National Revenue, and namely those of Sherbrooke, said that the act of Parliament was no good and that the legislation concerning bureaucrats is the valid one. They say that rendered services are not deductible. And it should be noted that they refused to refund some taxpayers certain amounts claimed as gifts to political parties, namely our party. Maybe the same thing happened to other political parties.
Mr. Speaker, The Royal Canadian Mounted Police was even used to intimidate our respective constituents, the Mounties went into the homes telling the electors of taxpayers that they were thieves, that they had submitted false returns and that if they did not sign a document to the effect that they had not helped the party, they would be thrown to jail!
Right on!

Mr. Speaker, if the RCMP want proofs, I have witnesses in my own riding where they went one night to the home of Mr. Maxime Lord, 2345 Saguenay Avenue in Noranda, and his wife, my chief organizer. Take note of this: two RCMP agents went in saying that they were liars, crooks, that they had lied to National Revenue, that they had claimed $200 which they had never given the party. The devoted work of those people, Mr. Speaker, is worth much more than $1,500 or $2,000 a year; but the two Mounties, two youngsters, went in there calling them liars and thieves. Fortunately, my two fellow-citizens, who are not easily intimidated, told them in turn that they had better sit down and be polite otherwise they would get thrown out! Then, things calmed down somewhat.
That is not the general reaction!
No, indeed, everyone would not greet them that way. Mr. Speaker, when that happened, I went to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) in this House, I went to his seat-
He's never understood anything!

How true! He told me that there had been anomalies, irregularities that some of our people were not honest.
That is what Solicitor General Allmand said to me, and I challenged him to prove it. Anyway, the whole file is in the hands of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) who said that he was not aware of the matter, that he would enquire to his official to ascertain what had happened, but that the whole matter might be in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen). I went to see the Minister of National Revenue at his seat and asked him a progress
Legislation
report on the matter. The minister told me that the file had been sent to his office but that it had been returned to the Minister of Justice, who, in turn, would return it to the Solicitor General.
Mr. Speaker, as to the tax returns made in 1975 for the 1974 taxation year, some people were in fact granted the recognized deduction for donations to political parties, after which the RCMP was asked to inquire. The ministers know nothing about the whole matter: three dummies they are! Deputy ministers do know what is going on, and they are the ones who decided to sue people. Now, in 1976, we file our returns for 1975. Apparently, 1975 political donations are accepted more easily. That is not all: assessment notices are presently being sent to some taxpayers requesting them to pay back what they received in 1974 for donations made in 1974. What nerve the National Revenue people must have to ask for the repayment of amounts paid out after May 1975.
Mr. Speaker, it is surprising that the ministers should not be aware of that. At this very moment, we have three representatives with the chief commissioner of income tax to check the record-
The RCMP.

The chief commissioner of the RCMP, that's it, Mr. Nadon. Three of them are there this afternoon to check the record. What is in it? We will know tomorrow probably, or later today. But the trouble we are having, I realize that other constituencies may well have it too. I simply want to state that Parliament is being laughed at. We passed that legislation here in this Parliament to allow your constituents to give you donations deductible for income tax purposes, not from the taxable income but the income tax, the tax payable. The act was passed here. But bureaucrats say, you, members of Parliament, are not right. They are the first to come here and beg for salary increases, higher pensions, to live fatly at the expense of Canadian taxpayers while members of Parliament who are elected representatives responsible to the people are being laughed at by little secretaries in the office of the deputy minister or minor employees who actually rule the roost.
Mr. Speaker, I am talking about the elections act. There are others. The CBC, a Crown corporation-there are other Crown corporations-but the CBC was asked in this Parliament to be more explicit, more national, to talk more about the role of the Canadian Parliament. I will give you another rather recent example: on May 25, when the budget was tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). The whole Parliament was here. I am sorry I could not be here. However, my colleagues were here and most members also. That evening, on Radio-Canada, when the news came on, I said: Now we are going to hear about the budget. I listen to the news in my area; we have freedon of choice.
We have a television station, Radio-Nord Inc., which is affiliated to Radio-Canada. Therefore we have one alternative: either we turn off the set or we turn it on. That is our only choice and we must hear the news on Radio-Canada because there are no other stations. So, in the evening, I listen to the comments about the budget. In the afternoon some hon. members were locked in for 2, 3 or 4 hours

June 1, 1976
Legislation
before the budget was brought down at 8 p.m. My colleague for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) was one of those along with other Liberals, Progressive Conservatives and New Democrats who studied the budget beforehand to be able to comment on it in the evening. So, in the evening I listened to the commentaries. They introduce the budget, they talk about the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and then they give the comments by federal representatives of other political parties. I think my colleague for Shefford was asked to record a three-minute commentary which was taped in the afternoon or evening-
No, five!
-or a five-minute commentary on Radio-Canada-
In colour!

... in colour, besides. At least, they have it colour! Not our political colour, the actual colour. Mr. Speaker, in the evening, I think the hon. member for Shefford was allowed less than half a minute . . .
40 seconds; on channel 10, 4 minutes.
... 40 seconds on the government network and 4 minutes on channel 10, a Montreal private company's station. The other party representatives were not allowed more than 2 minutes.
Not even the Minister.

Not even the Minister. I do not think he even had his 2 minutes, the Minister of Finance! This is the measure of CBC's impartiality, a coporation which is totally independent from political parties as well as from parliament. That same evening, the Inquiry Commission on Organized Crime, CECO as it is called, was allowed about 7 minutes to show the notorious Dubois family from Montreal. What the hell can that mean in Winnipeg? How does that concern . . .
Halifax!
. . . Yes, Halifax!
There are Frenchmen there!

Or how do scandals in Montreal concern the people in Vancouver? Even in toronto, they do not want to hear about it. People have enough troubles of their own, they have no need for Montreal's problems. Mr. Speaker, those in charge of the CBC do not to give a damn about members of Parliament. They are the first to laugh at us, they are the first to send us to hell...
And ministers for that matter!

... yes, both ministers and members of parliament. They say "We may or may not give them coverage". Who in CBC are those powers who decide that? They are the same people who come here "wacking" for their votes, not thousands, but hundreds of millions, to pay for those pale-faced people in the CBC's

Montreal offices, for giving coverage to those awful organizations. "We must go everywhere, we must cover every organization", says the Corporation. And to every organization they go. But the CBC should be held responsible for the division that now exists in various regions of Canada. It was shameful the way Canada's Parliament was treated last week on the occasion of the budget speech, which is of concern to every Canadian. The CBC cast aside such a serious issue, in favour of the Board of inquiry on organized crime, to show Justice Dutil and witnesses stating that they attempted to kill someone, they sold marijuana or haschish or what have you, that they had a prostitution ring in Montreal. That is quality indeed to improve the standard of public morals. Directly on TV it went.
Do they say anything about Parliament, about the important role played by members? No, they do not give a hoot. And I will tell you why. Because we, members of Parliament, we are not named for life. We have to get elected. Come the next election, we cannot take it for granted, we are not elected for life but for one term only. There is a new election every two, three or four years. Who knows what can happen in four, three or two years from now? Job security, that is not for us.
Employment security is requested for the CBC employees, employment security in journalism, employment security in the damned bureaucracy, employment security for civil servants. By the way, there is something else I would like to say. From all the members who were in this House when I was first elected in 1946-49, only three are still here: the member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), the member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself. Out of 264 or 265, only three members from those days still have a seat in this House. This is to show that we know what parliament is all about.
If we are here, it is not because we had employment security but because we fought hard in each election. But I do feel a little bit sick whenever I hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), even rightly so, say: "We have to treat our civil servants well." Employment security and better salaries are things we hear discussed every so often. "When are we going to increase their pensions, pay them decent salaries, and so on and so forth?" Good enough. I agree that our civil servants should be well paid. However, whenever federal members who have no employment security ask for a small salary increase, the civil servant is the first to object. I just cannot figure that out.
Federal members are paid $24,000 a year. Some of our civil servants earn as much as $40,000, $45,000 and $50,000 a year and we are still asking salary increases for them. Whenever a small increase of $2,000 or $2,400 is requested or suggested in Parliament civil servants are the first to fight against it despite the fact that members of Parliament do not have any job security and are never assured of being returned to the House at the next election. As soon as members start talking about a possible increase, the press objects to it. The newspapers then say that the members voted themselves a salary increase for their expenses in their ridings. Mr. Speaker, why is it, if it is so interesting to be elected member, that those fellows from
June 1, 1976

the press do not run for Parliament? Why do they not come here to sit as members?
First because they do not have the ability and second because nobody wants them. Third, they should just shut up and show some respect for the Canadian Parliament instead of trying to ridicule everything that happens here, to ridicule the members of Parliament who do something, to ridicule the ministers in front of civil servants and deputy ministers. I have great respect for deputy ministers. The organization-
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his allotted time has expired. He may continue only with unanimous consent. Is there consent?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues but I think it is true, I just started to be good. Mr. Speaker, I shall not take too much of the time of the House but I had to clarify the role that Parliament must play in this country so that the bureaucrats "stay in their hole." It does not mean they should be ill-treated but they should be respectful of Parliament and the ministers. Today, we have a Liberal government but tomorrow I hope we shall have a Social Credit government.
But we should be respectful of the authority at a time when everybody complains about the lack of authority, the lack of respect for those who are supposed to administer public funds and the nation's business. Mr. Speaker, we should be respectful and we should start in the media for instance where they always call out for the freedom of the press, yes, the freedom to lie to the people as filthy beasts can do. It is the freedom to deprive others of their freedom. Let us see who is calling louder for freedom in Montreal: the common front, Charbonneau, Pepin, Laberge. What respect do they have for the authority? What respect do they show for the National Assembly in Quebec? Those people are stirring up public opinion against law and order. But the freedom they are asking for is the freedom to deprive others of it and to end up with the kind of freedom they enjoy in Moscow or in other socialist countries in the world where people no longer have the right to speak loud, to say what they have to say.
Mr. Speaker, thank God we have not reached this point yet in Canada or in the province of Quebec. Should we however let the bureaucracy get hold of power in Canada we will be in exactly the same situation as those socialist or communist countries in the world. Mr. Speaker, I want to add that all the world countries which have allowed their bureaucracy to gain power are in a desperate situation today. They would like to restore this parliamentary freedom which still exists in Canada, thank God.
Mr. Speaker, let the ministers take their responsibilities and we, parliamentarians, we, members of Parliament, let us require at least that government agencies be respectful of the Canadian Parliament. We have the duty to pass the votes concerning their salary, we are responsible for all
Legislation
these people. And we are going to allow those officials who work in small offices, in riding offices here and there, to make a mockery of us and tell us: Just watch, Mr. MP, your case will not be dealt with because you mixed it up with politics. Mr. Speaker, politics is not an electoral policy nor a party policy between elections. It is a government policy, a Parliament policy and therefore public servants should be respectful of members of Parliament. They should consider that the law has to be enforced.
I referred earlier to the electoral legislation. In this regard, I suggest it is time-and I draw the attention of the President of the Privy Council to it so that he stresses the fact to the bureaucrats of the Departments of National Revenue, Justice and the Solicitor General-that Bill C-74 be strictly enforced instead of being tampered with as these people are doing at present.
Mr. Speaker, the members, whoever they are, should demand that public servants perform their duties and give the results expected and required from them, not golf games, yacht trips or extra-parliamentarian activities. What we want from them are results reported in Parliament and then Parliament will be brought back into favour before public opinion; we want the mass media to be attached to Parliament, be made available to the Canadian public so there will be no more deceptions by individuals who want to destroy us instead of promoting the selfdevelopment of the country.
Mr. Speaker, my appeal is directed to the members of all political parties and to the government to assume its responsibilities and put bureaucracy at the service of Parliament which will legislate to meet the needs of the people.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which is before us-and I should like to remind the House of this-is not exactly the same as the subject which has been discussed so eloquently by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). However, I can sympathize with the hon. gentleman. Having been a bureaucrat myself at one time, I can understand the situation very well. Having been a bureaucrat, a member of parliament and a minister, I understand what he is saying.
I suggest to him, however, that we should preserve as an essential principle of our democratic system the notion that the government should be responsible for its acts. This is a principle which is sometimes extremely difficult to interpret; As my colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) said earlier today, there are circumstances over which ministers can have no control. However, I hope the House will agree that in general ministers should be accountable to the House for their actions, and this includes the actions of their departments. It is a principle which has been accepted by the government ever since I have had anything to do with it, and it has been adhered to on numerous occasions when the opposition wished to go behind the government and begin to deal with civil servants. I believe such efforts should be resisted and that ministers have a responsibility to the House for the acts of their departments as well as their acts in a personal capacity.
May I now refer to the very interesting remarks made by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) who is joint chairman of the Committee on Regulations and Statutory Instruments. I am sorry he is not here now. I should like to congratulate him and his committee, including the senators and, in particular, Senator Forsey who is the co-chairman, on the very useful work they have been doing. They have had some difficulty in defining what constitutes statutory instruments, but that is to be expected. I hope we can clarify this situation so that the committee can carry on its work effectively.
I was interested in the suggestion made by the hon. member toward the conclusion of his remarks, that iye might adopt new procedures to deal, not with the question whether regulations and statutory instruments are in the proper form and within the ambit of legislation but, rather, whether they touch on substantial matters which are of importance to policy rather than simply to the carrying out of a statute. The suggestion that we might set up a procedure to carry the matter further if the statutory instru-
ments committee felt certain regulations were of such a character as to justify a closer examination in another standing committee is one which I would not reject out of hand. I believe it is a proposal well worth considering.
Mr. Speaker, the motion in the name of the Social Credit party deals with two matters, the first of which has not been debated at all, as yet. Neither the first speaker for the Social Credit party, nor the hon. member for Temiscamingue made reference to this part of the motion. I would remind the House of the terms of the motion itself- the first part. It reads:
That this House finds highly deplorable the attitude the government has demonstrated by taking advantage of its majority to draft many of its bills in such a way that different matters are dealt with in a single text-
In other words, as I understand it, the motion condemns the government, for bringing in omnibus bills. I believe the House is right to be cautious when asked to consider bills which cover a number of unrelated matters. But I suggest the government has been careful when bringing forward what are loosely called omnibus bills to observe consistency and confine the subjects to closely related matters.
I could pick out one or two pieces of legislation to illustrate my point. One is the measure presently before the House, Bill C-83, which deals with certain aspects of the criminal law. It has one theme-measures to provide greater peace and security. If it is argued that it would have been better to have brought forward a whole series of amendments by way of separate bills, I would answer that not only would we have found greater difficulty in dealing with the essential and urgent legislation which is before the House, but we would be repeating the debate on each of the items of legislation. I suggest the government has done the House a service by bringing forward in one bill amendments to the Criminal Code concerning peace and security.
I should also refer to another bill introduced some time ago early in the session, Bill C-16, dealing with the status of women. That bill did amend eight separate statutes, but the common theme was to provide equality of status for male and female persons. Surely the House would not have thought it desirable for the government to have introduced eight separate pieces of legislation simply because the bill purported to amend eight existing laws.
Various speakers, particularly the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants, have referred to the rules of procedure of this House. As President of the Privy Council and, for the time being, chairman of the House committee on procedure and organization, I should like to express my hope that we will bear these considerations in mind when we are dealing with changes in the rules which are now under consideration in the committee.
We do not as yet, in my judgment, have rules that enable us to deal effectively with the legislation that comes before this House, nor with the bills that we are being encouraged to introduce nearly every day to deal with other matters and for which we have not the legislative time. Moreover, I thought the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants was quite right in saying that under our present rules we do not have adequate time to deal with what he called the subordinate legislation made under existing statutes.
June 1, 1976

I believe that these comments are well justified. It seems to me that in this House we often substitute length of debate for careful consideration. There are so many occasions when an attempt is made to hold up legislation rather than to bring it to a conclusion and reach a decision. I can understand, Mr. Speaker, the desirability of giving the public time to understand the nature of the proposals that are put before the House so that members of parliament can get the reaction of the public; but there comes a time when an excessive dependence upon that particular principle simply inhibits this House from doing the job for which its members were elected.
I am quite satisfied, in my own mind, that this is not a contest between the government and the opposition. So often it seems to me that the proposals that are made for changes in the rules are represented as an attempt by the government to push its legislative proposals through the House. I, personally, do not think that is so, nor that the opposition should look upon it in that light. Perhaps some day they will be in government and will understand the problem from our point of view. If they work hard and show responsibility, they will have a better chance in the future, I suggest.
At any rate, one of the problems I feel we have encountered in amending our rules is that there are stereotyped reactions to proposals. The opposition says, "This is a government move to expedite undesirable legislation", and they take that attitude toward it. In the United Kingdom, where the rules are so much tighter and there is much greater control over time in the House of Commons, there is very little difficulty on that score because the two major parties alternate in office and know that one or the other will either be in government or in opposition at some time in the future.
May I also point out that there have been changes in the rules which enable us to deal much more successfully, and with less risk, with omnibus bills-for example, the provisions now in the rules enabling us to bring matters back into the House at the report stage. This was not so easily done in the past. Prior to this rule change, bills were considered in committee of the whole. But as someone has pointed out, there is a great deal of difference between considering a bill in committee of the whole and voting upon it in the House. Nowadays, a member has the right to put down amendments at the report stage and these are voted on individually and a recorded vote is taken. This is why omnibus bills can be dealt with more effectively than they were in the past.
I could say a good deal more on this subject, Mr. Speaker, but I believe hon. members are familiar with the problem and the changes that have been made in our rules enabling us to deal with omnibus bills without risking the possibility of dealing with a whole series of unrelated matters in a single piece of legislation.
Another development that has occurred recently and which is reflected on the order paper is the introduction of a bill to deal with technical amendments of a non-controversial character. This will be, in the truest sense, an omnibus bill. It will deal with many, many statutes. I look upon this-and I think the House should, too-as a very great improvement in the procedures for dealing with legislation. I hope in the future it will avoid the necessity
Legislation
of bringing in a whole series of minor bills to correct technical errors.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to the second part of this motion, which deplores the "obvious tendency to extend the scope of regulations under which pieces of legislation are to be implemented ..We are all aware of the increasing complexity of government. I should like to read to the House the opinion of one of the acknowledged experts on parliamentary procedure, Professor J. R. Mallory, who appeared before the special committee on statutory instruments on April 29, 1969. He put the problem forward in very clear language, and this is what he said:
The development of delegated legislation is one of the things that is necessary in the kind of modern urban and highly technological society in which we live. But necessarily parliament itself does not have the time or the capacity to produce all of the regulations which are necessary for the regulation of living in modern conditions. It is more important that parliament should devote itself to the big questions and keep a constant and wary eye on major questions of policy.
This, of course, was not in the beginning. At the time of confederation we lived in what is commonly called the night-watchman state. Nobody thought in those days that much regulation was necessary to protect the essential interests of the citizen. But now so much needs to be regulated to protect our health and welfare and safety because of the complexities of travel by air and sea and land, because of the need to develop provisions for the health and welfare of people under modern urban conditions. Also this kind of regulation by its nature requires very often rapid adjustment. We cannot live forever with a set of regulations about aircraft safety which were designed in 1918. We may have to change them with some rapidity. So that parliament simply has to delegate the power to make many regulations to subordinate bodies in the executive: ministers, government departments, the Governor in Council or some other kinds of Crown agencies.
That is the nature of the problem, Mr. Speaker. All of us who are members of parliament, including the government, may deplore the necessity to delegate in this way to ourselves, to our agencies and to other bodies the right to make subordinate legislation. But when we come to deal with practical issues that are facing us, we really have no other alternative.
That is why I believe the arrangement of the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments and Regulations was a great step forward. First of all, it reinforces the government's own efforts to ensure that regulation is within the authority granted by parliament. Secondly, it does open the way for a review of what is done under this subordinate legislation.
As I have said, I thought this was a very useful suggestion made by the co-chairman of the committee, that there might be some new procedure developed which would enable a committee of this House, if not the House itself, to have a look at substantial measures enacted under regulatory authority.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we now have a system whereby all orders that have legislative effect are tabled here in parliament, are automatically referred to the standing joint committee and are also published so the public can know what is being done. So we have established the machinery:
I do not think we in this House can ever be less than very wary of the extending power of government. We must always be very careful to ensure that it is this House of Commons which makes the ultimate decisions. I must say,

June 1, 1976
Legislation
however, that there is no way-indeed, even if all the rule changes I might favour as a member of the government to promote the reaching of decisions on government proposals were to be adopted-by which this parliament could avoid granting to the government delegated authority, because it could not legislate in time to deal with the changes that arise because of changing circumstances.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to enter this very high-level debate during which we shed our partisan clothes and look at this resolution of the Social Credit party on this opposition day, at the time when we are apparently pressed for time in dealing with more important matters facing parliament. I must admit, with the greatest deference to the Social Credit party, that I find some difficulty in interpreting the subtlety of the motion, particularly when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) referred to the fact that the lead-off speaker for the Social Credit party had not been speaking with reference to the motion. My own interpretation and assessment of the motion leads me to the belief that there is virtually nothing which could be said in this House today that would not come within the ambit of the resolution. It is a very broad resolution indeed.
This is a resolution which deplores a tendency which I think any member who has any sensitivity toward this institution would have to assume is a downgrading of parliament and this institution. I say that without pointing the finger of accusation at this or any other government. It deplores the tendency to, in fact, abdicate our responsibilities as parliamentarians by accepting the suggestion far too often that we should delegate responsibility by way of regulation and by other orders to the civil service or members of the public service of Canada. This is one thing that certainly has impressed me in my short time as a member of parliament.
I have had what I suppose is the distinct pleasure and honour of serving on that Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments and Regulations, referred to many times by the President of the Privy Council. I like to mention on each occasion we have a debate relating to that committee that it was my initial impression that the whip of our party, who is now my seatmate, sent me there for the purpose of administering a form of punishment, in the belief that a new member had to go through his own form of purgatory by sitting and looking through the mounds and mounds of regulations and orders in council which are promulgated by the government from time to time.
I was rather interested, from that point of view, in determining what kind of experience we have had in Canada in respect of the enactment of regulations and statutory instruments. The information I have from the Canada Gazette, part II, indicates that during the period of years from 1972 to 1975 there have been a considerable number of regulations promulgated. To give the House some idea of the scope and the extent of this delegation of power under statute to officials of various departments, it is interesting to note, for example, that in 1972 there were no less than 580 regulations and statutory instruments published in the Canada Gazette. In 1973 the figure was 755; in 1974 there were 560, and in 1975 there were 780. This is a very substantial number of regulations for any govern-

ment, let alone the government of Canada, to have promulgated.
This does not tell the whole story. The fact of the matter is that in addition to these documents which are published in the Canada Gazette there are, as yet, an undetermined number of orders passed which have the effect of regulations affecting the citizens of our country on a day to day basis.
As I indicated at the outset of my remarks, I think there should, and will be, on both sides, of this House a general approval of what I perceive to be the intent of this resolution. It is not good enough for the President of the Privy Council to have pointed out that we have, in terms of parliamentary time, simply not enough opportunity to deal with the technical aspects of legislation, or that things are getting so complex in the society of this country that we have to turn over the responsibility of passing regulations to the bureaucrats, the civil servants and departmental officials. That is an oversimplification of the situation and an easy "out" for the government.
We must be extremely vigilant in parliament regarding this growing tendency which is a very easy way for government to deal with matters. We must try to encourage the government to propose legislation which has not just a skeleton or bare-bones outline of principle but, rather, gives us in some reasonable detail the kind of information we, as parliamentarians, require in order to make a proper assessment of the merits of the proposed legislation.
One of the prime and most important pieces of legislation we have dealt with in current days, it seems to me, was the legislation relating to the anti-inflation program and the Anti-Inflation Board. I do not want to go over that debate as the facts have been repeated on a number of occasions. However, I think this is a good example of the situation.
We now see the anti-inflation legislation in operation. The Anti-Inflation Board and its administrator have been given a mandate under the act. We find that parliament has effectively lost control of the anti-inflation program, with the exception of one or two instances where the government of the day feels inclined, for whatever reason, to give instructions to the board or the administrator. When this happens, the government does so as though it were infringing or impinging upon a god-given right of the Anti-Inflation Board.
The government seems to take the attitude that it wants to avoid any form of leadership in respect of decisions by that board, sort of removing itself from the political considerations that go into the decisions of the Anti-Inflation Board. It seems to me that in the legislation creating the Anti-Inflation Board we have a prime example of legislation that affects the vast majority of the people in this country and the country itself in terms of its future economy.
We find that although the bill consists of very few clauses, it contains an important clause relating to the ability of the governor in council to pass regulations to give effect to the over-all principle which is stated in, practically, one clause of the bill. It refers to the government's intention to fight inflation. It seems to me that this

example and the resolution of the Social Credit party at this particular time, when we have had an opportunity to assess the work of the Anti-Inflation Board over a period of some months, at least gives us an opportunity to consider the direction in which we are moving in respect of this kind of legislation, and an opportunity to remind ourselves of the general alarm we all felt about the Prime Minister's statement about the end of the year in which he said we should continue to look at a new society with the idea that perhaps controls might be a way of life. We should take a second look at the situation on this basis and hope that we will be able to bring this concept to an end before the next election.
As I have said, I wish to keep this above partisan politics, so I mention that merely as a possibility. The fact of the matter is that there have been some fundamental changes in parliament over the years. I had the opportunity to work, not as a civil servant, as did the President of the Privy Council, but as an executive assistant in the government when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister. At that time I had an opportunity to observe the role of parliament and the role the opposition played in that whole scenario.
I recall that the government at that time had a majority consisting of 208 members. I believe there were something like 48 or 50 members of the official opposition. I remember very well the situation at that time. In those days there was a very fundamental prerogative of parliament which now has been removed. I refer to the whole question of supply. I remember when the ministers came down to the treasury benches, to pass their estimates, how concerned they were about having to face the opposition at that time because the opposition had the right to withhold the granting of supply until such time as answers were forthcoming from the ministers concerned.
Simply because I am a member of the opposition, I am not suggesting we should have any greater rights than the government. However, I suggest there is a role the opposition plays in the parliamentary system, although the idea apparently has now being given up of returning supply to the House and giving the House the ability to withhold the granting of supply. This idea of returning supply to the House is not a bad idea at all. We have had the experience of the past few weeks and months of seeing ministers delegate their ministerial responsibility.
I suggest to the government House leader and to members of the cabinet who are present today that some of the problems we have had may not have arisen if, in fact, supply had remained in the House and if, in fact, the ministers were not in a position to slough off their responsibilities. As I say, some of the problems we have had would not have occurred had we had supply in the House and an opportunity for the opposition to withhold supply by carrying on the debate. Of course, the opposition has a responsibility in this regard because of the need for supply to go forward at a certain time and because otherwise certain people might not be paid.
As I say, that is a responsibility which rests with the opposition. I suggest that the minister, at least, should be in the position of having to answer for the activities of his own department and not be in a position to slough off any part of that responsibility by saying he received improper

or unreasonable advice from some poor career public servant.
I think it is unfair, as we saw today, for the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) to suggest that a public servant in his department, Mr. L. H. Stopforth, had given him wrong information. I wondered then, and I wonder now-aloud-whether it is good practice for a minister to get up and simply blame someone under his authority and have him moved to another position, as opposed to the minister taking the full responsibility for his department and suffering the consequences even to the extent of tendering his resignation if his department is not functioning.
I think we will pursue the whole question of ministerial responsibility on subsequent days, because it is not clear to me that the Minister of Supply and Services is completely fault-free in this regard. There are other circumstances which have come to our attention which indicate that the minister either did know or ought to have known the full circumstances of the LRPA negotiations and should not have used one of his civil servants as a scapegoat in order to avoid responsibility for his department.
As I say, I intend to deal with this motion on a nonpolitical basis. I am sure hon. members opposite will agree that I am doing very well in this regard. I think our committee system, which is part of the over-all process of government, is relevant to the motion the Social Credit party has brought forward. One thing I have noticed since I have been here as a member of parliament is a tendency, which I do not recall being apparent at the time I was here previously as an executive assistant, of ministers not to appear even when their estimates were before the standing committees but, rather, to send their deputy ministers.
I notice that there also has been a tendency to send deputy ministers to field, and occasionally attempt to answer questions of policy. I think, first of all, we should take a look at this development in respect of our committee system. If we do not have supply in the House of Commons, I think at least the minister should appear at each committee meeting, without exception, to deal with matters of policy. If the hon. member opposite thinks it is an exception to the rule when ministers do not appear, I suggest that he look at the situation in respect of legislation. The tendency there is to have the deputy minister appear and answer questions concerning particular legislation. I could give an example of occasions before standing committees when a member of the public service has come in and has been asked questions relating to government policy or, as we refer to it euphemistically, departmental policy.

You cannot have it both ways, and I agree with the minister that when you open up the proposition that deputy ministers and civil servants are going to be speaking on behalf of the government, you should be consistent and have it right across the board. All I am saying is that we in parliament should give consideration to whether this is in accord with the parliamentary tradition we have in this country. Should we be allowing deputy ministers to answer on questions of policy, or should it be the strict responsibility, with some sanction attached, of the minister always to answer and to be advised by his civil servants and his deputy minister?
I simply pose that, not in a partisan manner, but simply to point out that the tendency, at least while I have been here, has been to have the civil servant appear before these committees, and I wonder aloud whether that is a good development as far as our parliamentary practice is concerned, and whether it does not lead to some of the questions with respect to ministerial responsibility which have arisen in question periods and in debate in this House over the past few months.

As I understand the Government of Canada, the cabinet gives leadership and the opposition tries to give constructive criticism. I suggest that the overriding responsibility of any government I know is to initiate legislation so that it can be considered by Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition and other opposition parties for the purpose of their giving constructive criticism. However, in this case a tendency which I do not appreciate has been followed with respect to Loto Canada. It has been a tendency to shove this particular initiative through the back door.

I see that you are moving to your feet, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion may I say that I appreciated the opportunity of participating in this debate, but I did want to make that one point with respect to Loto Canada. I would have thought the government would have had a sense of responsibility and leadership, and would have brought forward specific legislation so that we would know exactly what we were getting involved in and so that we could argue the merits of the case. Unfortunately we have been denied this right, and I think the Social Credit resolution, for that and other reasons, should be supported.

Mr. Speaker, anyone following this debate today without making reference to the motion which has been put down might not know what it is we are discussing. The amount of time which has been spent debating the actual terms of the resolution has certainly been at a minimum.
There are a few things I want to say which I think are related to the essence of the motion, but first I want to take three or four minutes as an individual member of parliament to protest very strongly against the attacks made in this House today on public servants.
Hear, hear!

I not only resented those attacks, I also resented the amount of applause which came from government supporters across the way when those attacks were made. We were told that public servants treat members of parliament with ridicule, that they laugh at us, and that they tell us where we can go. I have been in this House of Commons for more years than any other member except one, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I want to say that I have never been treated with discourtesy or lack of respect by any public servant. Like other members of parliament, I have a great many dealings with them. I write them letters, I call them on the telephone, and I go to see them.
What about judges?

I do not telephone judges. If I telephoned a judge, I hope he would say something critical.
My friend, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), is sitting here. I pick him out because he is here, as he is so often, and I pay tribute to him for his attendance.
Hear, hear!

He can be
proud of his officials. As he heard me say in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs the other day, I think he has a tremendous staff in his department. I deal with them a great deal. I deal with the chairman of the Canada Pension Commission, with the chairman of the War Veterans Allowance Board, with the chairman of the Pension Review Board, with those who are charged with treatment services and with the Veterans Land Act and all the rest of it.

What about members? What about respect?

I am sorry that my hon. friend has not understood me. That is exactly what I am saying-my experience is that the public servants treat members with respect and courtesy. I object to the tirades against them this afternoon.
Part of this motion has to do with the multiplicity of regulations, the amount of governing that has to be carried on in that way. I have the same concern as everybody else that there are too many regulations and that too much is done by way of order in council and regulations. But when you have an operation as gigantic as that required to govern 22 million or 23 million people, an operation that is carried on by 250,000 or more public servants, you cannot settle every last detail in this Chamber. You have to delegate some of the authority to make some of those decisions.
That leads me to say that I think one of the most important statements made this afternoon was that made by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) about the way we use our time in this House of Commons. It is a plain fact that we cannot deal with everything. That being the case, I hope we may yet come to the point where we can use our time to deal with the most important things, the major issues of policy. Let us deal with them here on the floor of this Chamber. The ministers should be responsible to this House, but let us face the fact that details will have to be worked out at the administration level. As the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants pointed out, that means we must find some way of coping with the problem of time.
The President of the Privy Council and others can turn up certain pages of Hansard and show where at times I have resisted the government's attempts to impose closure or the use of Rule 75C. I simply say to them that my aim is that we come to a means whereby we can co-operatively decide on the use of our time. What I cannot accept is one side saying how we should use our time. To me that is closure or dictatorship. We must have enough sense on both sides of the House to plan the use of our time so that we do not waste it in great lengthy debates on unimportant issues, and thus deny ourselves the right to debate issues that are really important.
I have said that I think a government should tell us at the start of a session what its total program is. The government pretty well does that now, except when it keeps the session going for two years. Then we have lost track of the beginning of things. Having given us the list of what is to come before us, then the opposition parties should have the right to pick four or five items on which we want unlimited time. In return we should agree that there are 10, 15 or 20 items that are so routine they ought not to have debate in the House at all but should go to second reading committees, consideration in committee, and even third reading outside of the House, and in between the very crucial issues and the relatively unimportant ones there are issues to which we could give some maximum time limit.
The purpose of this is not to accommodate the government-although the government is always seeking accommodation-but to accommodate parliament so that we have time to deal with the major issues and not feel, as is being expressed so many times today, that we do not get at the issues and that therefore the public servants are doing

It is a form of taxation, in my view; it is not levied according to ability to pay, it is levied according to the instinct for gambling, the desire to win something for nothing. The result is that the tax bears heaviest on the poor.
The first time this parliament of Canada goes in for that method of raising public funds we are doing something pretty crucial. For it to be done in a way other than the standard practice of a bill that comes into parliament, has second reading debate, committee debate, and third reading, is scandalous. For the minister to say there can be debate in the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates is begging the question; to say that the opposition can bring it back on an opposition day-since when does the government get out from its responsibility to bring its measures before parliament?
What happens is that the government wants this; the government is boss; the government is king; the government is God. It wants Loto Canada, and it sees it is not going to get it by the end of June through the normal process of bringing in a bill so it brings in a supplementary estimate, shifts it to committee, and knows through the way things have been working this month that come the end of June it will be back here in a supply bill and we will not have a word of discussion about it on the floor of the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, I submit that is playing fast and loose with the way this place ought to operate.
That is all I want to say today. At first I was not even sure I would take part in the debate. I also want to protest again the way in which the government is bypassing the normal processes of parliament with respect to a change in the methods of raising money a change which I think is very sad.

Mr. Speaker, as I said before supper, the motion presented by the Social Credit Party of Canada was in fact motivated by their frustration in the face of bureaucracy.
As a matter of fact, they situated the problem within the parliamentary context and stated that backbenchers, which they all are, had serious problems whenever they wanted to discharge their responsibilities as ombudsmen, law-makers and spokesmen for their constituents. I feel justified in discussing this question, Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) has shifted the debate in that direction. I admit that there are rather serious frustrations and that the number of civil servants has increased quite significantly since World War II.
Of course, it has become obvious from the questions they put on the Order Paper, that the members of the Social Credit party are really anxious to see that their constituents avail themselves of all the programs. Of course, they are aware, as I am, and as are all hon. members, that there has been an increase in the federal programs of assistance to the electors. I need only mention the LIP projects, old age security benefits, family allowances, and subsidies to the farmers. I could spend hours listing them. Of course, such achievements require a substantial increase in the number of civil servants.
Actually, some way must be found to monitor those people more efficiently. One need only mention the method used here, that is, questions that are put on the order paper. This year, Mr. Speaker, over 5,642 of them were put on the order paper. Improvements are necessarily needed. But the information used can help hon. members in their questions to the ministers, either here in the House or in the committees of the House.
It is obvious that if in answer to a question an hon. member is satisfied to be told how much money has been spent in his riding, he will not have enough information to
