speechtext:
As for those who think that actually the House of Commons is no longer interesting, they are totally wrong, Mr. Speaker, since the major part of the federal government's business is carried on in this House and the major decisions made by the government are echoed here. It is also here in this House that the government replies to the accusations brought by the opposition and it is here that we account to the country for the management of the public affairs of Canada. All I ask the members of the opposition is to admit that the best way to let people know what happens in this House is to use the method acknowledged by everyone as the most sophisticated, the most advanced information media, that is television.

I wish to thank members of the Social Credit Party for giving the House the opportunity to engage in such a wide-ranging debate. I am sure no two members have talked about the same issue since we began this afternoon. It shows the importance of the place this House holds not only for the members of parliament within its precincts but for the electorate generally and all Canadian citizens wherever they may be.

June 1, 1976

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate and to have the opportunity to congratulate my hon. colleague for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) for presenting this motion.
I would like also to thank all hon. members who have spoken so far for taking the trouble of learning more about the procedures and orders of this House. I would like in addition to reassure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Center (Mr. Knowles) that, in my humble opinion, the motion put forth by my colleague for Shefford was not intended to blame civil servants but rather to draw the attention of the government on some of the powers of bureaucracy. I for one can vouch for the honesty, sincerity and devotion of most if not all federal civil servants. Besides, the remarks I intend to make shortly will not aim at blaming civil servants but rather the present government and the preceding ones, which, in my view, gave far too much latitude to some high officials.
This being said, Mr. Speaker, the question that i would like to raise now is who is leading Canada, who is conducting the affairs of the country?
In general, I think it is not difficult to admit that senior officials and bureaucrats are now managing the business of our beautiful and big country, either by interpreting our legislation according to their views or sometimes by passing the legislation which they consider more convenient.
As all members of the House know very well, since 1969 the Parliament in Ottawa has had a committee whose duty is to consider all regulations. It is usually called the Joint Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. Its duty is to review all regulations normally called "delegated legislation" to make sure that regulations are not contrary to the British common law. By the way, I must say that I am not altogether against regulations, but the fact is that when those regulations are drafted by bureaucrats, they should come to the House so that the legislators might compare the regulations and the legislation and, if the former sometimes take precedence of the latter, the legislators should have the power to correct them.
We must find out whether those regulations do not actually violate the British common law, the Bill of Rights or the intent of the statutes themselves under which they are enacted, because their contents may never go beyond the terms of reference stated in the delegating statutes. Therefore it may be considered that in some way the so-called "delegated legislation" is also "subordinate legislation".
In 1969, the committee headed by Mark MacGuigan, member for Windsor-Walkerville, made an inquiry into that matter. I would like to show, through statistical data, the numerical importance of the process of delegating authority. To illustrate, I shall quote from the report by the House committee that inquired on that subject in 1969, concerning the extent of regulatory powers delegated to the federal Civil Service:
The administrative authorities and their staffs play an important role in the preparation of the statutes enacted by Parliament itself, since that vast majority of legislative proposals originate in the Administra-
Legislation
tion. However, it is also now commonplace for the Administration to make laws directly, without having to observe the complex but safeguarding rules of parliamentary procedure.
Four hundred and twenty of the 601 Acts of Parliament examined by the Committee (constituting substantially all of the statutes now in force) provide for delegated legislation. Moreover, a substantial majority of the answers given to question No. 2 of the Committee's questionnaire stated that statutory powers to make regulations have been used very extensively.
The following statistics confirm this impression: 6,892 regulations covering 19,972 pages were published in the Canada Gazette during the period from January 1, 1956, to December 31, 1968, an average of 530 regulations a year. This does not take into account those regulations which are expressly exempted from publication and also some documents which are perhaps in fact of a legislative nature but are not officially considered to be so by the regulation-making authority.
So during the past 22 years, 6,892 regulations were published in the Canada Gazette, included in the unbelievable number of 19,972 pages of the publication. Let there be no amazement if I state that most of those regulations covering a number of fields have been and still are in force unless abolished or superseded by others, without ever coming before Parliament.
I remember a few particulars: in 1969, 638 regulations were passed; in 1970, 540 regulations; in 1971, 656; in 1972, 564; in 1973, 729; in 1974, 676; in 1975, 709; and up to May 12, 1976, 291 regulations were passed. In all, since 1969, 4,803 regulations were passed for the federal administration, 600 per year on average in the past eight years. As far as Quebec is concerned, it is felt that there are as many.
Indeed, excluding the numerous municipal by-laws in force at the present time, the following data taken from au article by Mr. Raoul Barbe in the Revue du Barreau, on page 386, give some indication of the quantitative significance of the phenomenon of delegated authority, and I quote:
The development of the rule of law by the excutive is an important source of law, since in 1972, there were some 1,400 pages of legislation while the regulations covered over 3,000 pages of the size of the Quebec Official Gazette. (A) search has permitted the consolidation of some 950 regulatory texts (in effect in 1972) covering nearly 8,000 pages and published in 10 volumes known as the Legislation Implementation Regulations.
About 450 regulatory texts are approved annually by the Executive Council and about 150 regulatory texts are approved by other regulatory authorities: either a minister, the Treasury Board or a regulatory board.
Now, after demonstrating the qualitative importance of regulatory power delegation, I would like to show the qualitative importance of this delegation of powers by using an example taken from the War Measures Act which reads as follows:
(1) The Governor in Council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada: and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it is hereby declared that the powers of the Governor in Council extend to all matters coming within the classes of subjects hereinafter enumerated, namely, (a) censorship and the control and suppression of publications, writings, maps, plans, photographs, communications and means of communication; (b) arrest, detention, exclusion and deportation; (c) control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada and the movements of vessels; (d) transportation by land, air, or water and the control of the transport of persons and things; (e) trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture; (/) appropriation, control, forfeiture and disposition of property and of the use thereof.

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I believe that we should urgently get involved in this area, as we are being invaded by bureaucrats.
The Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments I referred to earlier came to the conclusion, to nobody's surprise, I think, that a great many pieces of legislation do not proceed from legislators but from senior officials, bureaucrats who earn $30,000, $40,000 and $50,000 a year. Mind you, I have nothing against such salaries.
Mr. Speaker, only Parliament can pass laws, but they are so vague that for the ordinary citizen, the noble disign of the elected representatives is very often less important than the restrictive regulations established by officials hanging out in their ivory tower of Tunney's Pasture or Wellington Street, or elsewhere in the national capital.
Before going any further, I would like to quote from a speech made by the hon. Guy Favreau, former federal Minister of Justice, on January 11, 1965, before the Lawyers' Club in Toronto and entitled: The State, the Citizens and the Ombudsman:
Our laws are more and more like preambles. The detailed provisions remain to be drafted and amended at will by public service experts.
You know no doubt that quite often the law authorizes bureaucrats to make regulations. At first, the regulations seem less formidable than the statutes in general, but it can be said that the difference lies more in the words than in reality. The great majority of regulations passed by this House are in effect and quite simply because they can be enforced by officers or still by the court. I would like to give a rather concrete example, more specifically section 172, 4(b) of the unemployment insurance regulations. Unemployed are divided into three categories-unfortunately one is excluded, and I refer to farmers. That regulation provides that 50 per cent of the farmer's net income is deemed to be gains, even if his operations are in a deficit position. I think that is illogical and unfair, and I do not think this is what the legislator had in mind. In any event, that is not what I had in mind, I can assure this House.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that the purpose of today's motion is not to deny the necessity for the government's regulatory action because, in the first place, it is readily admitted that Parliament does not have time to draft all regulations that become law, on the one hand, because Parliament does not have the technical knowledge and, on the other hand, because it does not have the flexibility and the capability to make quick and wise decisions. Suffice it to think only of two bills now being considered, Bills C-83 and C-84, to realize that it takes sometimes two, three or four months to consider a bill.
No, Mr. Speaker, this motion is aimed rather against the huge volume of regulations and particularly the dangers inherent in that legislative effort. Consequently, I would like to refer to the third report of the House of Commons Special Committee on Statutory Instruments, dated 1969, that is the MacGuigan's report which reads as follow:
The more fundamental of the criticisms can be summarized as follows: the parliamentary tendency to enact statutes in skeleton form, leaving the "details" to be filled in by regulations-such regulations being often the very matters that are of most importance to the citizen; uncertainty in enabling statutes as to the extent of the area regulations are intended to cover; sweeping or subjective terms used in enabling acts which exclude the judicial control of the regulations made under their authority; lack of public debate, and inadequate consultation of all

interested parties before the making of the regulations; lack of precision in the form and content of the regulations; inadequate publicity given to the regulations ...
In other words, not much publicity. There may be some about legislation but when it comes to regulations nobody even hear about them. I continue to quote:
... inadequate publicity given to the regulations after they are made; inadequate parliamentary control over the regulations; and the danger that civil servants may be transformed into our masters.
As a matter of fact, it is possible that the great activity of the government could have serious consequences and in saying this, I think of the fact that bureaucrats could one day direct the people they are supposed to serve.
Mr. Speaker, what is the percentage of regulations which are passed by high officials and which are sent to committee? In fact, I cannot answer that question now but I would be very surprised if there were many. In my humble opinion, the regulations are the servants of the laws and they should not receive more consideration than their masters. I sincerely think that the government must in the future submit to Parliament all the regulations drawn up by the bureaucrats so that the hon. members may get acquainted with them and debate them as openly as possible before they are enforced.
At present, the civil servants are rather more responsible for the government of our country than the representatives whose role is consequently less and less important. The civil servants have the opportunity and full discretion to draw up regulations which are often inconsistent with the spirit of the laws adopted by Parliament. Once again, I sincerely think that the present government must take all the necessary corrective measures so that members of Parliament will no longer suffer from the interference of civil servants, I mean the bureaucrats, and also to restore to them all the dignity they deserve.
Another point draws my attention, namely the various committees which are created. What is the real use of the hundreds of committees which are supposedly created to solve the various economic and social problems? Their only use is to spend the money of the people as a reward for the privileged classes of the present system. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is unbelievable to see the slump in which all the classes of our society find themselves. For example, in Quebec, it is not by setting up all kinds of committees that the future of Quebecers is going to be decided, because if we consider one moment the seriousness of these committees, of the inquiries launched by governments, we note that it is only an orgy of spending, of useless redtape, a waste of human energy, and all these committees cost millions of dollars. And with what result? Those who pay the bill would like to know!
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak about the staggering increase in the number of civil servants in Canada in the last few years. Before World War, I, around the turn of the century, the Canadian government employed an army of 23,000 public servants or so who were responsible for the administration of our beautiful country. A few years later, during World War I, it could be noted readily that the number of public servants had doubled, which was understandable since the country was going through a national crisis, and insurrection. But, since that time, one realizes that the population of Canada has

I want to thank my colleagues for granting me a few more minutes. I will try to be brief, Mr. Speaker.
I was saying that we note as well that the strength of the public service, except perhaps for Crown corporations, is made up of 300,000 people, that is an increase of 1200 per cent or so.
Mr. Speaker, surely it is during World War I that Canada has witnessed the fastest increase in this area-there were then approximately 46,000 public servants. Some time later, around the end of World War I, the number of public servants which was, as I have just said, about 46,000, had come down to about 40,000.
Thereafter, it has been noted that the strength of the public service remained constant until World War II. As soon as this one broke out in 1939, the number of public servants more than tripled, while continuing later on to show an upward trend.
But it must recognized, Mr. Speaker, that it is under the administration of former Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson, for whom I have always had a lot of respect, that the federal state in which we are living has taken the most new initiatives and that the growth of the public service as such has shown the highest rate.
Besides, it is easy to realize when we know that Canada has now at her service about 1,200,000 Canadian civil servants, that is one worker out of eight or 12 per cent of the labour force. How much does it cost the state in salaries and annual payments? Around $10 billion a year or almost 13 per cent of our gross national product. One can say therefore that government is the sector of the economy with the fastest growth. One cannot deny the fact that governments, whether at the municipal, provincial or federal level, is one of the most important tools in our country and is easily competing with the service sector, the manufacturing industries and so on.
When the right hon. Prime Minister came to power in 1968, the total number of civil servants was 50 per cent more than what it was in 1960. Then, in 1969, when the Trudeau government was fighting inflation, our Prime Minister promised the country to reduce the number of public servants by 24,000, or about 10 per cent. Once again, in its usual manner, the federal government broke its promise and after a whole year, it barely managed to eliminate 535 jobs, or one-fifth of its original objective. Later on, one could see that the public service had rapidly regained the lost ground.
Mr. Speaker, we are not in a state of national crisis and we wonder why the red tape is taking as much expansion

as if we were in war time? According to University of Toronto Professor Richard Bird who had the opportunity to study these questions for the Canadian Association of Fiscal Studies, this constant race would be the consequence of pressures or of the tolerance of the public who demands more and more services from the government, influenced by politics or by officialdom. But does the Canadian taxpayer who demands more and more services from his government realize that he is thus putting himself in a position where he has to pay more taxes?
The hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised at the subject chosen tonight by the Social Credit party of Canada. There was a time when the Social Credit Party of Canada would speak only on the monetary question. Perhaps this choice shows a new maturity, a new skill in the House or again perhaps a closer link with the Progressive Conservative party? I do not know.
Hear, hear!

But I am a little surprised at the choice because it seems to me there were such excellent choices. I would have thought perhaps the Social Credit party might have chosen the common fund, for example, which is a monetary question and we could have had paraded before us this evening the unedifying spectacle of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) being dragged silently screaming, commodity by commodity, digging his heels at every commodity, into the common fund of the Third World, protesting all the time that that is what he really intended to do from the beginning. Or perhaps we could have had a resolution on the special drawing rights being discussed at the UNCTAD Conference at Nairobi and the special drawing rights in relation to the Third World because that, Mr. Speaker, is the closest thing to social credit the world has seen since Mr. Aberhart printed his own script in Alberta.
There are other areas that might have made a choice for the Social Credit party this evening. On the other hand, they have proposed this interesting motion that finds highly deplorable the attitude the government has demonstrated by taking advantage of its majority to draft many of its bills in such a way that different matters are dealt with in a single text. That I would submit, although unusual perhaps coming from that direction in the House, nevertheless is a problem for us all and one that deserves our attention this evening. I think the members of the Social Credit party have done us a service this evening by putting the finger on a problem which is not only a parliamentary problem but one which has widespread ramifications for the Canadian public.
I should like to mention, not bill by bill, a few of the topics which have been so-called omnibus bills. We had a
June 1, 1976

Legislation
bill on abortion and I think the public saw it as that, but it contained a number of other things as well. After it was passed I think many citizens were surprised by some of the other things that were removed from the criminal law, or placed in it, through the passage of that omnibus bill.
More recently we had a bill which at the same time combined rape and bail. It had an interesting passage through the House. I do not think the two subjects were served equally by their inclusion in the same bill. I should like to refer to the bill on citizenship which was not really an omnibus bill although it presented some of the same problems, because while it removed sex discrimination it also reduced the waiting period for citizenship. I know some members who were opposed to the second of the two clauses in the bill were criticized for holding up some very worth-while legislation to remove sex discrimination which has been on imposition on women in this country for many years.
One of the most flagrant and the most recent is the bill known to the public as the gun control bill, but known to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) as the bill on peace and security. While I do not wish to renew the debate on that bill which has been passed on to committee, nevertheless I might say that this relates to the subject of the motion. The problem that besets not only the House but the public is that the bill dealt with such disparate subjects as gun control, wiretapping, and dangerous offenders, all in the same omnibus bill.
There is a lack of clarity in the public's conception about what is happening in the House and what is before the House. I am quite sure that when the gun control bill is out of the way a good many people will wonder when if ever did parliament deal with wiretapping and dangerous offenders. There will be a sense that somehow those important parts of the omnibus bill did not receive the sort of treatment they should have, because one part absconded with all of the attention.
It is terribly important-and here again I think the Social Credit people have done us a service-that in the legislative process the public not see something as having been traded off for something else. Yet increasingly this is the perception. It is not a very flattering perception either of the government's ability to draw up legislation or of the way this Chamber should function. Never has the trade-off been so blatant as in Bill C-83. One would have a suspicion that the government, having tried omnibus bills a few years ago and finding that they work, has been using them increasingly until it has realized that it could get passed through this House something that would not normally pass this legislative body by combining it with enough other factors, with enough other issues. It would seem that the government realized that in this way it would be carried along because there would be a reluctance on the part of members to seem to oppose some rather worthwhile bits of legislation.
There is another thing I should like to mention as well, that is, the certainty that parliament has passed the unpopular part, that when one part receives too much attention then there is a losing sight of the fact that the other went through as well. One of the problems the Canadian public has at the present time is the sense that what is the law of the land did not seem to have been
observed going through parliament, and yet was carried along in the wake of some popular items.
The real question always remains, do we really learn the will of parliament when it is confronted with four, five, or six highly different items in the same bill? Each of the items is defended by the government in committee, and although the government House leader talks about the opportunities which present themselves at the report stage to amend, I have found that by the time the government has shepherded its bill through second reading and through committee stage there is a fierce determination that no further change shall take place at the report stage.
I think the government House leader is suggesting something really quite illusory, almost as much of an illusion as that which was presented to us a short time ago by the deputy House leader when he talked about television in a way which was irresponsible at worst and terribly funny at best, when we consider the role of that technological marvel in North America at the present time.
This situation is particularly abhorrent when the government has a majority. There may be some excuse for this practice during minority governments. Some of the legislation which was discussed was put through in minority situations, but if the government has a majority I think it has a responsibility to present legislation which is clear cut, to defend it, and to see that it moves through parliament. The responsibility then is where it should lie.
The government House leader said the government should take responsibility for its actions, and I say "Amen" to that. Of course it should, but if it were really accepting the responsibility it would separate some of these items and put them through on their own merits instead of putting them through with something else.
Let us consider, for example, the amendments to the Criminal Code which dealt with rape and bail. The hole in the Bail Reform Act was so appalling and the things which were happening as a result of people charged with murder obtaining bail, and of people charged with drug offences being able to go out on bail to continue their trade, were so appalling that there was a great need for a rapid movement of that legislation through parliament.
However, with regard to the section on rape I have a feeling it did not get the full and complete treatment it should have had, and having sat last weekend in Nanaimo and listened to some women's delegations there I know that they are not happy with the law on rape as it now stands. I think it is unfortunate that in order to plug one hole with a desperately needed amendment something else was moved through which will now remain on the books for quite a few years as rather bad law. This is one of the penalties the government and the country pay for this kind of preparation of bills.
No more clearly is this evidenced than in Bill C-83. I attended a meeting about a month and a half ago at Invermere, and the large public gathering there voted unanimously to urge that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) separate the gun control sections from the rest of that bill. I passed that on to the Minister of Justice, and he replied saying that Bill C-83 as a whole is aimed at protecting the public against violent crime and that as legislators

we cannot present one bill for law abiding citizens and another bill for the criminally inclined. That was not at all the request at the public meeting to which I referred.
They asked clearly, as this party did through the efforts of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), that the gun control section simply be removed so that it would not be discussed along with wiretapping and dangerous offenders legislation, and so that parliament could deal with that one main issue free from the responsibility of the other two or more sections in that omnibus bill dragging along at the same time. We know from the furore those sections stirred up across the country that the public was very much in favour of having them separated. It does not matter what else happens to Bill C-83; it will always be known as the gun control bill. The words of the minister were particularly ironic because the bill does have something to do with law abiding citizens because they are being asked to bear an added load for the sake of the criminally inclined. Put together with Bill C-84, in a double back-to-back package, the situation becomes almost intolerable.
I think it would be better if the ministers would caution themselves and prepare pieces of legislation which are more specific. I feel that in the end it would shorten debate in this House rather than lengthen it. There are some bills-for example, the revision of the Bank Act-which will be before us in a year or so-which are enormous in themselves, and not much can be done about that, but it makes little sense to load up the legislative docket with maxi bills which contain so many clauses that many of them are almost lost sight of as they move through the House.
With regard to regulations, hon. members from the Social Credit party also have a point because too much is dealt with in this way. An example is Bill C-83. We members of parliament have to go out and talk to the public about such bills. We are asked how much it will cost, how often it will be applied, whether it will be varied according to the weapon, and what will be meant by due care in locking these things up. If we members of parliament over and over again have to say we don't know and that we will have to wait until the regulations come out, eventually this institution will begin to look a little ill informed generally, and we will again run into a problem which results from the approach to legislation which has been used far too much already and is being used too much in this parliament right now.
Examples of legislation which have to be separated are the redistribution bills and the Canada Elections Act. I am sure if this were not laid down by long practice and tradition, the government would have lumped the Canada Elections Act and the redistribution bills all together, along with several other items. If the government could have rounded this up in time, put it together and presented it all as one great mess to this parliament, it would have done so, but by the very nature of the redistribution bills and the process which has been traditionally used, this has to be dealt with province by province, and certainly that marvellously clarifies the debate on that rather far reaching move.
I think a service would have been done to parliament and to the country if several of the recent omnibus bills
Legislation
had been divided into their separate clauses and dealt with as individual bills, certainly none more so than Bill C-83. We know that it was only through the strongest protests from this side of the House that we did not get one single bill dealing with the abolition of capital punishment, the extension of prison sentences, gun control, wiretapping, and dangerous offenders. It was not planning on that side that sorted it out but only a fierce determination on this side that the abolition of capital punishment at least should go. Even then, it was sadly messed up, and as we debate it now on second reading we see the government was not prepared to put it as a central issue.
Again the government weakened and succumbed to the temptation to trade it off for the greatly lengthened prison sentences that are of concern to many serious thinking people in this country. Even there, Mr. Speaker, it was a clouding of what should have been a very simple, very straightforward bill on one topic and one topic only.
I congratulate the members of the Social Credit party- in a way they surprised me but did not displease me in presenting this motion to the House. This is a problem to which I hope the government will pay a little more attention. One thing is for sure, as long as this sort of general untidiness is presented to this House then televising the whole mess will not improve it in any way.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I think this is an interesting resolution. It condemns the government in its majority position for producing bills that are not conducive to the understanding of hon. members.
The first thing we should do, if anybody is serious about this, is examine the bills produced in the last minority parliament and compare them with bills produced in this and the previous majority parliament. If we did we would find that the form of the bills and the content were not changed at all. Basically the same kinds of faults are found in bills produced in either a minority or majority situation. It seems to me, if you make the effort to look at the quality of the bills, it must be something deeper that causes bills to be written in such a way as to give rise to this motion and debate. I submit there are indeed a number of pressures at work which cause bills to be written in the way they are.
Without any difficulty at all I think one can identify at least five different kinds of bills. The first I would categorize as those which establish something new, something we did not have before. An example would be the creation of Petro-Canada or the Petroleum Administration Act. The first establishes a new institution and the other sets up the mechanism for an administrative tribunal.
The second kind are those which I would classify as amending acts. We have had a number of those in this parliament, perhaps the most prominent being the amendment to the Anti-Inflation Act. We have already passed a series of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. These acts may touch on a number of points within the main act, some of which may be related and some of which may not be.

The third kind are those which provide new provisions within an already existing legislative framework. Perhaps the most prominent one in the last few years was the amendments to the Canada Elections Act, called the Election Expenses Act. In this case we grafted something totally new onto the framework of an existing act.
Lastly, we have what might be called omnibus bills. Perhaps the most flagrant examples of omnibus bills are those we get after each budget. These are the bills that deal with the amendments proposed by the Minister of Finance-the sales tax in one sequence, in a second bill all the amendments proposed to the Income Tax Act, and in a third bill a set of amendments to the Excise Tax Act. These are omnibus bills in the true sense because those amendments will touch on a variety of things and have almost nothing in common except that they are presented by the Minister of Finance as part of a budgetary package. So it is with the ideas behind the peace and security package. They present a series of ideas in a package framework for amending the Criminal Code and are designed to deal with certain problems.
One of the problems we have in the House of Commons is that all members of parliament want to be loved; we do not want to vote for anything that might be nasty or might not have the unanimous support of our constituents. We do not want to vote for those things that may be necessary to accomplish certain aims and so we find it extremely difficult to vote for packages, some parts of which we may agree with and some parts with which we may disagree.
The point is that in the imperfect world in which we live we often do not have that kind of choice. We have to take some of the imperfections along with the perfections, and the perfections that I might see in a particular bill are not necessarily going to be the same as any of my colleagues on either side of the House might see. Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. It is never that way so much as when one is contemplating legislative packages.
The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that if you look at what is going on you will find that the government behaves in the same way in a minority situation as in a majority situation when it is drafting and presenting legislation. The main pieces of legislation fall within the five categories I have given, and there normally is something to tie them together.
The previous speaker complained about amendments to the Citizenship Act when he was prepared to vote, according to him, for the amendments within the act dealing with sex discrimination, but had certain reservations about that provision which reduced the length of time a person had to be in Canada in order to apply for citizenship. That is an amendment to one act which is part of a package series. It does not seem fitting to me that it would be necessary for the government to present two legislative sets of proposals to deal with a series of amendments to one act. Surely you have to take amendments to the act and look at them as a package, because you are dealing with an already existing package and are providing amendments to it.
The way our system operates, members have an opportunity to vote for or against individual components on two occasions, once in committee at clause by clause consideration, and in the House of Commons there is the opportunity at report stage to vote against specific clauses. There

is also the possibility of doing something in limited fashion at third reading.
I think if one looks at these speeches tomorrow, judging from what I have heard today, one will find that the fundamental problem members have, which has elicited this complaint from members of the Social Credit party, is a dislike of the way in which the House of Commons utilizes its time.
As an example, opposition parties have 25 days on which they are allowed to dictate the business of the House. We have set it out in our Standing Orders so that five days are used in the first term, seven days in the second term, and the rest in the third term. That means that 13 opposition days are jammed into May and June. This is simply too much, and we do not use that time properly. We should revise our Standing Orders so that this time is used more evenly throughout the year.
Instead of ending up in a situation where we run out of ideas and start seeking things to talk about because we have too much time at a particular point in our procedural year, we should be revising our Standing Orders so as to spread opposition days on an equitable basis throughout the year. That would leave the opposition parties far more flexible, and it would leave the government far more subject to attack by the opposition parties. It would be much better for the health of parliament. That is an example of what we have done in our Standing Orders.
Let me look at bills, Mr. Speaker. If one looks at the way bills are handled in the House of Commons it is important to realize that, by and large it is the opposition parties which dictate how much time is spent on legislation. The function of the government in our system is to produce an agenda of work, or bills, on which the House is to decide. The job of the opposition is to determine how much time we shall spend discussing each piece of legislation and which portions of the legislative package it wishes to comment on and object to. That is only proper and right. Taking any piece of legislation and dividing it into 25 separate bills does not mean that this process will change. Members will still pick and choose the parts on which they wish to comment.
One of the most difficult decisions we must make in any reform of our procedures is to decide how long the House of Commons shall sit, and how much time we are prepared to spend in the House. As members of parliament we have duties other than sitting in the House. In the last eight to ten years the average session has lasted 180 sitting days. Do we want to sit more than 180 days, or less? How long do we wish to sit? Further, how much legislation is the government to be permitted to bring before the House? I am speaking of legislation in addition to work already allocated to us under the Standing Orders. The question is, should the government be allowed to bring in 70 pieces of legislation, 80, 100, 50 or 40? How can we decide how long the House should spend discussing each legislative proposal unless we first decide how much time is available? Only then can we decide how much time to spend on each item.
As an institution one of our big faults is that in allocating the time we spend on legislative proposals we do not distinguish between what is important and what is not

important. If you listed all legislative items on a priority scale running, say, from one to ten, you would find that we probably spend as much time discussing items low on the priority scale, say, occupying position No. 10, as we do on items high in priority scale, say, No. 1. This means that we are not really thinking about how we ought to operate this institution, and not thinking of how to get the best results for our time and effort.
Let me now deal with the point raised by the Creditiste speaker who preceded me concerning the question of regulations. This House, in Canada, produces legislation more detailed than that produced by any other legislative assembly in Canada. Anyone examining legislation passed by the provincial governments of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta, or any other province will find that such legislation is loosely defined, which means implementation at provincial level is a matter for the cabinet. Usually it is done by way of regulations. On the other hand legislation we pass is most detailed and, because it is detailed, much of it must be amended each year. We face this problem because the government, in order to bring such legislation up to date, must constantly change legislation previously passed by this House.
After all, society is not static. It changes. The focus of our concern changes. People move; economic conditions change, and legislation and the impact of legislation must also change. You can do this two ways. You can ask the cabinet to make the changes or you can bring the legislation back to the House of Commons for amendment. In our system we use both methods, probably on a 50-50 basis. That is why, as the hon. member preceding me said, we have established the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments. It tries to keep track of regulations and the statutory instruments which flow from the cabinet, to make sure they are compatible with the legislation on which they are based. The committee has a difficult job to do and is, I think, doing a fair job. It is difficult to say how successful it will be in the long run; at present we have to give it full marks for enthusiasm and effort. But our difficulties will not go away. We must amend existing legislation to make certain that the law reflects the changes taking place in Canadian society.
Considering the overcrowded agenda of business with which parliament must now deal, and the ever increasing demand for time to be spent on ever more legislative proposals, it becomes most difficult to justify putting more detail into our legislation. I argue that this process entails trade-offs. Members on all sides accept more regulations as the price for the privilege of playing around longer than necessary with legislation going through the House. We can sing to our heart's content about what is in the legislation and what is not, but if we take more time than is really necessary we are allowing the government more regulatory making powers. I feel this is a bad bargain.
I feel that the House should examine the agenda placed before it and put more pressure on the government to produce its legislative list. We should know far in advance what bills we are to discuss so that we can sit down together, as a group, and work out an appropriate timetable, then ensure it is covered by an order of the House so that we can all know what is to happen. Not only will we
Legislation
settle many of our difficulties in terms of length of debate but we shall all discover far in advance what is to happen in the House. At present, apart from opposition days and budget debates, there is no way of finding out what is to happen here on any given day.
We are given no document on a daily basis which tells us that some matter is to be taken up at three o'clock, five o'clock, or eight o'clock. We operate by guess and by gosh. This is not good enough for an institution as big and as complex as parliament. That ought to change. But we can only eliminate the problem when we decide finally to move into the twentieth century. We must deal with the problem of the parliamentary agenda, with how much time we are to spend discussing government legislation and how long speeches are to take, so that we can program our time in a way which makes sense to us and to the Canadian people.
I recall when the House of Commons sat one summer, shortly after I had been elected to this place. I was visiting my constituency and somebody asked me "Well, Reid, what are you doing? I guess you are enjoying your summer holiday?" I said, "Hell, no, the House of Commons is still sitting." He said, "Do you mean to say you guys are not smart enough to be able to take the summer off?" Mr. Speaker, we do not get any marks for staying here because we have wasted our time. That only indicates our own inefficiency.
Then why is the government keeping us here?

When we hear people making comments about the House of Commons we wish they would not make, we must take a certain amount of responsibility. We are in the dark ages when it comes to deciding what we should do with our time, and how much time we should allocate to the consideration of all our business to make sure there is fair disposition.
My last point concerns the changes to which we should look forward in order to bring us up to date. It seems to me that our legislative style can change only if we move to the point at which all members of the House understand what the government's legislative load ought to be. That means that we would need to put certain restrictions on the government. We should try to determine how long in any given year the House of Commons should sit. That would put restrictions on us all. We should also decide how long individual members should speak on any given item, and the length of speeches could vary from item to item. One can see the foolishness of permitting 40 minute speeches on second reading and 20 minute speeches on opposition days. There is no logic to it. Perhaps we ought to limit speeches to 15 minutes; we ought to deal with that problem.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the fine oration by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). He talked about a topic that he thinks he knows, procedure in the House of Commons.
We hear government members speak on this topic, and members of the opposition parties. It is unfortunate that we never get a balanced argument. For example, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River referred to the fact that there are 25 opposition days, 5 in the first semester, seven in the second, and so on. He neglected to explain that in 1969 a majority Liberal government introduced those proposals and forced them on this House of Commons by closure. Now he is trying to say that the House did all this in a very nice way. That is not quite the fact. If he had explained further and given the proper perspective, there would have been more truth.
The hon. member also stated that the opposition sets the timetable. Although I was not a member of this House in 1969, I recall reading in the papers that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the government was going to introduce all bills at the beginning of the session so that the opposition would have an opportunity to examine them. That has never happened. The Prime Minister does not force his cabinet to do that.
With regard to bills that are to be dealt with before we adjourn for the summer recess, a week or so ago there was talk about two bills which the government desperately wants passed, but which members of the House have not even seen yet. If it so desperately wants them through, it should table them. In fact all bills should be tabled at the time of the Speech from the Throne, unless there is a genuine emergency. That would be a rare occasion, and a rare bill.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River tried to put the onus on the opposition. He did not mention that in 1972 there was an election. To a large extent that revolved around unemployment insurance. The government remained in power with 109 seats and the major opposition with 107. Even though the election was on October 31, the government did not convene the House until mid-January. What happened to November and December? I guess there was no urgency.
There was another election on July 8, 1974. The government always talks about its timetable and how it wants to get things done. However the House did not sit for the remainder of July, August or September. In fact it did not sit until October. We could at least have associated ourselves with school boys and girls and commenced at the

beginning of September. The government must bear certain responsibilities which it does not bear at the present time.
One of the great concerns of the opposition is that the government uses railroad tactics to get legislation through the House. An example is the Time and Reader's Digest bill. The committee was frustrated. The committees do not work in the way they were intended. Concerns must be expressed on the floor of the House of Commons.
There were a number of government members on the committee which considered the Time and Reader's Digest bill. Some had been on that committee for two years. In fact one had been the chairman. The government removed them from that committee because they were going to oppose the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member has mentioned an area over which I have some responsibility in the committee. No one was replaced on that committee unless they were absent at that time.

Governments in general, and this government in particular, like to run the country by means of orders in council,

regulations, directives, and so on. Ministers try to get rid of the burden of being in the House where they must answer to members from all parts of the country. They would rather the bureaucrats run everything with some tangible or some intangible control, depending on how effective a cabinet minister might be. In the area of awarding contracts, they make sure that the right person receives them. This puts the cabinet in a more powerful position and keeps members of the House away from issues of concern. This is a substantial weakness in our democratic process.
Over the years governments have tended to use regulations, orders in council, and a number of other procedures to get around passing substantive law, or amendments to substantive law. It would be preferable for the government of the day to introduce short bills, possibly housekeeping bills. If necessary there could be a time limit such as that in Great Britain. However, a bill should be brief and deal with only one topic.
Making regulations or orders in council and having them published in the Canada Gazette is not a good way of reaching decisions which affect thousands of Canadians. Most Canadians do not see the Canada Gazette-they would probably be bored to tears after reading the first page of it if they did. These are not laws or guides for conduct which have been passed after discussion in the public forums such as the House of Commons. Regulations and orders in council are passed after private discussion in cabinet committee or in the cabinet as a whole. The public ends up not knowing about them.
I am particularly pleased that the Social Credit Party should have introduced this topic. It is a most worth-while subject of discussion because it goes to the core of our democratic system. The resolution expresses concern on two grounds, the first being that the government introduces omnibus bills. The second is that too much power is exercised by means of regulations and orders in council. With regard to the second point, which relates to an extremely debatable area affecting not only members of parliament but all the people of Canada, may I remind the House that in 1972 there was an election and that the government just about lost its right to sit on the treasury benches. One of the key issues in that election was the unemployment insurance fund.
Back in June 1973 the government announced its intention of introducing two bills on unemployment insurance. The first was to provide some $800 million to cover a deficit which had been hidden during the election campaign because the party opposite did not wish to explain that they had been dipping into the till to cover runaway costs. The second was Bill C-125 which would have had the effect of cutting out many of the misuses of the scheme. In a speech on television in the Kitchener area on February 3, 1973, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated that Bill C-125 would be introduced into the House within a few weeks.

I represent a constituency where unemployment happens to be running around 22 per cent in one community. Generally the unemployment rate is about 10 or 12 per cent. Then there was the election of 1974. I should like to ask whether the people of Canada know what is happening under the regulations which govern this scheme. In fact, the purpose of these regulatory powers is to give a greater administrative latitude to the executive, which is necessary and which has been recognized by many countries. Hon. members are probably aware that in France, for example, the National Assembly legislates only in extremely general matters and leaves it to the executive to implement the general principles so that the regulatory power is excessively wider than the power our executive enjoys in some circumstances only, when it is expressly provided in the statutory instruments.
Thus, this regulatory power is not a problem as such except that the statutory instruments in question ought to be reviewed periodically in the House of Commons and this is the role the Committee on Statutory Instruments gave itself or which has been attributed to it and I think it does an excellent job. If we continue in this direction, we shall come to a situation where Parliament will approve legislation containing generally a page or two, and then an agency made up of public servants will prepare under the form of regulations hundreds of provisions which will modify the form, the spirit and the scope of the original legislation.
Mr. Speaker, there is another example that I would like to give, even if several members here tonight perhaps found the motion of the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) ridiculous, that is an act that was passed in Parliament and to which 90 to 95 per cent of all members, including Liberals, Conservatives, New Democrats and Social Crediters, were strongly opposed, the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, when we, the Parliament, had given a commission full power to redistribute the ridings. Several members, including myself, had to drive distances of 500 miles to represent about 60,000 people.
This commission has now submitted a project which, for myself, gives me about 800 miles to drive in my riding to serve a population of about 88,000 people. However, an exception has been made concerning part of the constituency which was not included in the 1971 census, but the people of this area would like a representative who can serve them. I believe that all hon. members will agree that the spirit of the legislation that we passed was very "grand", and that it is not only Parliament which will suffer, but especially constituents who will have to choose a representative in the next election.
Mr. Speaker, another issue has created a lot of controversy among the population. It is Bill C-83 now before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-RATIONALIZATION OF TRANSPORT POLICY WITH OTHER PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
TRANSPORT-RATIONALIZATION OF TRANSPORT POLICY WITH OTHER PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-RATIONALIZATION OF TRANSPORT POLICY WITH OTHER PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: TRANSPORT-RATIONALIZATION OF TRANSPORT POLICY WITH OTHER PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am grateful for the support. Obviously members realize the importance of the question that was raised last Thursday and that I wish to raise at a little greater length this evening, having to do with co-ordination of transportation policy and the sensitivity of the government at the present time to the situation in respect of transportation problems in the Atlantic provinces.
This is not new information, I assume, either to the minister or his parliamentary secretary who will be responding this evening. However, I would be less than frank if I did not say the comments last week by the Council of Maritime Premiers, and the appearance of the P.E.I. minister of tourism at one of our standing committees in Ottawa on Tuesday, gave a real indication of the depth of anxiety and, perhaps, the extent of neglect that currently exists in respect of those transportation problems in the Atlantic region.
First of all, I wish to elaborate slightly on the question I put last Thursday. I wish to place on the record some quotes from the communique from the most recent meeting of the Council of Maritime Premiers. Incidentally it was the fifth anniversary of the Maritime Premiers' Council, which is a most valuable body in terms of effective policies and programs for the three maritime provinces. In their communique the premiers said they were requesting an early meeting with the federal Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). The communique stated:
The premiers re-affirmed their position that transportation systems should be used by governments as positive tools for the attainment of national and regional objectives ... They stated that despite the federal government's agreement with their position, there is an alarming lack of hard evidence that transportation is, in fact, being used as a positive development tool. Indeed, there are examples of just the opposite .. . The premiers expressed concern that the federal government is increasing cost recovery within some transportation systems without considering the effects of this on the over-all economy.
Later on in the communique we find this:
The premiers expressed disappointment that a revised intra-regional freight assistance program advanced by the Atlantic provinces to the federal government in February of this year had not as yet received an official response ...
The premiers expressed disappointment in the federal budgetary restraint program as it applies to transportation expenditures.
Members will recall that the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) then asked a question in terms of this particular part of the communique. The premiers

June 1, 1976

took issue with the discriminatory nature of the transportation sector of the announced program, noting that of a total reduction of $41.2 for the whole of Canada, $21.9 million or 53 per cent would affect Atlantic region transportation programs exclusively.
If we just think for a moment, this means that in fact over half the reduction in expenditures directly affected Atlantic transportation where we have somewhat less than 10 per cent of the population. Considering the frequent occasions on which the federal government has paid lip service to the idea of co-ordinating transportation policy with its regional development program, this seems at the least to be shortsighted and perhaps even somewhat disastrous.
The premiers concluded their statement with these words:
In view of the present economic situation in the Atlantic provinces and the effect which transportation has upon it, the announced allocations of transportation expenditure reductions was deemed to be inconsistent with programs designed to correct regional disparity.
That was on Wednesday last week. The previous day when the P.E.I. minister of tourism appeared before our Standing Committee on regional Development he said a number of things having to do with the difficulties he had encountered in co-ordinating federal-provincial policy in the area he administers, but in referring to the over-all problem of co-ordination of federal-provincial programs he said:
We could spend the complete afternoon discussing these in details, but I will simply say that there is not much evidence of co-ordination policy-making between federal entities such as the Ministry of Transport, the Canadian Transport Commission, the Canadian National Railways, Air Canada and Parks Canada, just to name a few.
I will not restate the question I put the other day, but all of this seems to fly in the face of what the federal government has announced for some years as its prime intention. I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members a paper presented in November by Mr. H. Ropertz, a member of the transport policy task force on the matter of inter-governmental co-operation in transportation policy. I shall quote two or three things from that document because it is an indication of the commitment at the official level in respect of dealing with the transportation problem in some sort of rational and sensible way.
He said there is, and I quote:
... a growing realization on the part of the federal government for the need to consult and not take unilateral action, even though jurisdiction at times is federal.
He went on to speak about a specific federal-provincial committee, known as the Federal-Provincial Committee on Atlantic Region Transportation, which was organized as far back as 1969. That is an important date because it followed the passage of the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act, the establishment of a new national transportation policy, and perhaps more important, the establishment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The committee has been composed of senior federal and provincial government officials from the Ministry of Transport, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and from the provinces of New Brunwick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward island.
He went on to say that although the committee was mainly concerned with transportation problems as they affect their specific regions-and he was speaking, in effect, about three similar committees-one of the most
Adjournment Debate
significant aspects of the terms of reference of each of these committees is that they are working toward economic or regional goals and objectives. He also said that the idea that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) would sit down at least two or three times a year with each individual member to go over progress and tackle pressing problems was envisaged.
If there has been anything useful raised in this latest series of questions, it may be the frank admission by the Minister of Transport that he was somewhat surprised that the premiers should be unaware of the steps which are being taken by the federal government to co-ordinate transportation policy with the provinces in the Maritime region, and perhaps adding to that surprise there may be additional encouraging information from the parliamentary secretary about this problem this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-RATIONALIZATION OF TRANSPORT POLICY WITH OTHER PROGRAMS FOR THE ATLANTIC REGION-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy an opportunity to respond at this point during our proceedings to my friend, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), and I hope I can satisfy some of his concerns this evening.
Tonight, and on previous occasions, in at least a part of his argument he has suggested that the Government of Canada has disregarded a request by the Council of Maritime Premiers concerning the intra-regional freight assistance program. Rather than a disregard in this area, or in any of the other areas which have been touched upon by the hon. member this evening, there has been careful consideration of the position including, in the particular case of the freight assistance program, a possible position which had been generally agreed upon at one point between the Atlantic ministers of transport and the federal Minister of Transport with regard to freight subsidies.
In that connection the original idea involved a $5 million cut at one point in the subsidy and, as I have said, there was agreement on this point from the Atlantic ministers. Our combined hope was that the smaller amount of money thereby available would in fact obtain more positive results over-all. After further reflection on this point at both levels of government, and some assessment of the technical challenges involved in that original suggestion, it has now been concluded that the desired beneficial impact of the arrangement is not likely to be attained in the time frame available, and action on the whole matter has therefore been postponed to allow for further analysis and genuine discussion between the two levels of government involved.
There is certainly no need for the kind of anxiety which has been expressed this evening and on other occasions in the House. There has been every assurance that the Government of Canada is taking regional problems-in this case in the Atlantic region-very much into consideration. This has been made patently clear during the course of a series of very frequent meetings at the officials' level and certainly also at meetings involving the ministers as well. We have an ongoing and regular system of meetings in place and under way. This will continue in the hope that during the course of the summer, in relation particularly to the intra-regional freight assistance program, an appropriate program can be worked out to the satisfaction of all involved.

June 1, 1976
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-PROPOSAL TO GRANT EXPORT LICENCE TO SELL FISH OUTSIDE CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS OF PROCESSING COSTS
FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-PROPOSAL TO GRANT EXPORT LICENCE TO SELL FISH OUTSIDE CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS OF PROCESSING COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where is the minister? Where is the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc)? Does he dare send only a messenger? Sir, that characterizes the attitude of this minister with reference to inland fisheries since he has taken on the portfolio of minister of state. Not only are the fishermen in this country intimidated by having something less than a full ministry but the minister has refused to stand squarely in his place in the House of Commons and articulate his policy on inland fisheries.
I tell you, Sir, I give him full marks for going around the country and the world and signing agreements with all nations, but when there is trouble on the home front he ought to face it. On this very day the minister stood in his place opposite and challenged me to stand and give my position with reference to inland fisheries. Here I am, Mr. Speaker, and I want to know where he is.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-PROPOSAL TO GRANT EXPORT LICENCE TO SELL FISH OUTSIDE CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS OF PROCESSING COSTS
speechtext: He is with the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer).

subtopic: FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION-PROPOSAL TO GRANT EXPORT LICENCE TO SELL FISH OUTSIDE CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR ANALYSIS OF PROCESSING COSTS
speechtext:
No doubt. Mr. Speaker, I want there to be no mistake and no misjudgement. I do not want the parliamentary secretary to be in any way in the dark as to where I stand on this matter. The minister ought to look at the historic facts and their relationship to inland fisheries. The agreement-and I have it here tonight-signed on June 4, 1969, between the Government of Canada and the government of the province of Manitoba, in section 2(2) reads as follows:
The amount payable by the province pursuant to subsection (1) shall not exceed the sum of 25 per cent of $100,000.
That was the original amount of money-of capital investment by the federal and provincial governments to set up the inland fisheries known as the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act of 1969. That has grown from $100,000 to $5V4 million. At the time of the inception of the corporation it was signed by a minister of the Progressive Conservative party, the Hon. Harry Enns who originated the concept of a single marketing agency for orderly marketing. That was what the fishermen expected and that was the intention of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act, but this government along with its counterpart in the province of Manitoba, Premier Schreyer, and on June 25 twisted the act, invested $5!4 million, and decided not only to go into orderly marketing or a single desk marketing agency but also to get into the processing business.
Neither in this House nor outside have I quarrelled with the concept of orderly marketing. What I have quarrelled with, and upon occasion have asked the minister to justify, is the existence of a corporation in respect to the processing. This is fishermen's money, not tax money. The minister was dead wrong this afternoon when he suggested tax money was involved. I will tell you why there is federal tax money and provincial tax money involved; it is because this government-perhaps not this minister-set up and

spent $3'/2 million. I want to know who authorized that because the agreement was for $100,000. They blew it, Mr. Speaker. They could not administer it, and caused the corporation to lose $2 million in one year. The only reason federal tax money was involved was because they had to pick up what was their fault-not the fault of the fishermen.
I want to know who authorized the additional $2 million over and above the $314 million that was never authorized. I want the minister to answer that. I do not want his parliamentary secretary to stand up and give me some song and dance about how great the corporation is and how great the concept is, because it was my party that originated the concept. What I want the parliamentary secretary and the minister to answer is who authorized the $514 million. Who authorized the additional expenditure? I want them to agree to ask the corporation to open its books and do an audit-not the kind of namsy audit that the government is familiar with, but to answer the questions of the fishermen. This is fishermen's money and they have a right to know.
The minister claims to be the great knight in shining armour who fights the dragons that would gobble up the fishermen and their profits, yet refuses to give the kind of information that it is only reasonable to expect from such a corporation.
The fishermen want to know by species what it costs per pound to process the fish. Surely that is the right of people whose money is being used by this corporation. We are not asking for anything to be changed until we know the facts. If the minister who is in charge of the inland fishery as well as the offshore fishery refuses to provide that kind of information to the fishermen, he will be acting irresponsibly. I ask the parliamentary secretary, when he speaks on behalf of the minister, to answer this question: will he or will he not cause an audit to be undertaken so that, at the very least, the fishermen will know what they must pay to process their fish, and how those costs compare with those entailed in the orderly marketing concept?

Those problems loom so large that the province to date refuses to contribute toward the deficit of the corporation, something which no doubt the hon. member
June 1, 1976

knows. There are problems throughout Manitoba concerning transport costs. On each side of the hon. member each province was contributing to transport costs, but the hon. member's province was not. There are also great problems in northern Manitoba.

speechtext: Why does the parliamentary secretary not deal with my question?

speechtext:
There are also problems connected with marketing and production. The hon. gentleman talked about an offer which was made in Motley. Mr. Speaker, the corporation thanks the hon. member for the information and says it will investigate the particular offer. That, essentially, is what the hon. gentleman requested.
Essentially the corporation as it exists today enjoys the support of all the provinces concerned, as well as of the fishermen concerned who act through the advisory committee. It certainly has the support of every single fisherman who was fishing before the corporation was set up when there were great rip-offs involving distributors, collectors, and buyers in certain parts of Canada and the United States.
It is important to remember that the corporation cannot exist if its efforts are splintered here, there, and everywhere. The minister responsible for fisheries and the present management of the corporation, which is perhaps one of the best management groups ever to have been in charge of the corporation, are working consistently with all provinces concerned and the Northwest Territories to work out the best possible deal.
If the hon. gentleman were to ask fishermen in the general area covered by the corporation if they are generally happy with prices, I believe the answer would be yes, despite the existence of problems. There are problems concerning provinces which have production plants which produce final products. Some provinces do not have such plants. Therefore adjustments must be made, within the accepted criteria. But it would be irresponsible of the hon. gentleman to suggest that the corporation should be disbanded because of the complaints of a small group of fishermen, I believe 21 fishermen of a total of 300 in the Lake Winnipeg area.
