subtopic: AIR CANADA-ALLEGATION OF POOR BILLING PROCEDURES IN FINANCE BRANCH, WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT POSITION
AIR CANADA-ALLEGATION OF POOR BILLING PROCEDURES IN FINANCE BRANCH, WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coincidentally two Manitoba members this evening are asking for a proper audit of a Crown corporation. Of course the answer given to the request of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) constituted complete evasion. We are used to that.
Adjournment Debate
I have been asking for the Auditor General to conduct a complete audit of Air Canada's finance branch at Winnipeg due to the financial fiasco there, the huge deficits being faced, and the requests for fare increases. I received a most unsatisfactory answer from the Assistant Auditor General who stated, and I quote:
As you are probably aware, parliament has directed that the accounts and financial transactions of Air Canada be audited by the same auditor that parliament appoints to audit the accounts of Canadian National Railways. Therefore, in my opinion, the Auditor General has no authority to conduct any inquiry nor has he any right of access to the financial records or documents of the corporation.
That statement is completely false. It is signed by J. R. Douglas, Assistant Auditor General. I wish to point out to Mr. Douglas and the parliamentary secretary that under Section 67 of the Financial Administration Act the Auditor General can be appointed as the auditor or joint auditor of the corporation. However, that has not been done in the past. It is certainly time that it was done, especially with regard to Air Canada.
There was a report of the independent review committee of the office of the Auditor General which was completed in March, 1975. In that report it states that the Financial Administration Act defines a Crown corporation as:
-a corporation that is ultimately accountable, through a minister, to parliament for the conduct of its affairs.
When a Crown corporation such as Air Canada has a $12,473,000 deficit, an audit and accounting system that has completely broken down, and has the nerve to state they want a fare increase, the Auditor General should move in immediately. A directive should be issued by the government to have an immediate audit conducted. All the contracted work should be returned to the finance branch in Winnipeg. There were further recommendations by this committee. I quote from chapter six, page 116:
The Auditor General should audit the financial accounts of all Crown corporations whose expenditures directly affect the budgetary accounts of Canada.
On page 117 it states:
The Auditor General should have the right of access to the financial records and documents of all Crown corporations of which he is not the auditor, as he deems necessary to the fulfilment of his responsibilities as auditor of the accounts of Canada.
The Assistant Auditor General made reference to the auditing done by the firm of Cooper and Lybrand of Ottawa. In their submission to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), in the 1975 Annual report, they state:
Our examination included a general review of the accounting procedures and such tests of accounting records and other supporting evidence as we considered necessary in the circumstances.
We are not interested in a general review of Air Canada. We are interested in a complete and proper audit. This document should be questioned as to whether it is worthwhile. I imagine it was very costly, yet all we get out of it is a general review.
One of the issues I raised two weeks ago was the War-nock Hersey account which had 400 tickets not accounted for. The following day after I raised the matter in the House, Air Canada received a statement for $44,000. The parliamentary secretary informed the House that the account covered a period of several months. That was not

June 1, 1976
Adjournment Debate
correct. It was for a period of three years. All that was showing on Air Canada's books was $1,600 owing, not $44,000. That account has now been closed. Therefore it can be seen why the Auditor General should move into Air Canada. This statement has, I imagine, been supplied by Air Canada, so the parliamentary secretary will see he has been misinformed by Air Canada.
A further reason for the Auditor General to move in was given by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) during the question period today when he pointed out that travel agents are not adhering to Air Canada warnings about improper billing practices and procedures. My hon. friend first raised this matter on November 26, 1975, and the Minister of Transport has been most negligent in taking no action to rectify the problem. This is a matter which I myself have raised. I pointed out there are no longer any enforced controls on the reporting of ticket sales by travel agents. As of October, 1975, in excess of the 96,000 travel agent ticket sales were unreported. This represents a minimum of $2,208,000 unpaid for transportation. Air Canada's lowest fare is $23-this is the basis of the calculation by which the figure of $2,208,000 is reached. Further, billings to Air Canada from other airlines do not receive a complete audit inasmuch as items billed for $75 or less are assumed to be correct and are paid for without question.
I might say also that there are in excess of 180,000 tickets which have been used but in respect of which there is no record of sales ever having been reported to the finance branch. At a dollar a ticket this represents a lot of money, but when one considers that the lowest charge on Air Canada flights is $23 there is cause for concern to the tune of a possible $3,843,000. Can anyone explain the many hundreds of thousands of ticket sales which have been reported but in respect of which the fares collected are insufficient to cover the cost of the transportation used? I hope the parliamentary secretary will give a satisfactory answer tonight, along with an assurance that we are to see a proper audit and an end to this financial mess in Winnipeg.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR CANADA-ALLEGATION OF POOR BILLING PROCEDURES IN FINANCE BRANCH, WINNIPEG-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, in reply to the argument raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) this evening I hope I can offer some reassurance by making three or four brief points.
On the general question of the financial management of Air Canada, its auditing and other procedures, the House
will know that the whole subject was examined very thoroughly not long ago by Mr. Justice Estey, and his report, which was published last year, is a very helpful and important document. I know the hon. member has studied it closely and I know it has given some guidance to the government in connection with what future action might be taken to correct what difficulties or apparent difficulties were revealed in the course of Mr. Justice Estey's study.
The hon. member's second point has to do with the general accountability of Air Canada to parliament, or more particularly to a standing committee of this House. This was referred to, at least in passing, by the hon. member a few nights ago when he and I had an opportunity to discuss this same question during the adjournment proceedings.
The steering committee of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications has considered the question of an appropriate time at which to invite Air Canada to appear before members of parliament for a thorough discussion of the corporation's operations. I would imagine that such a discussion would include the subject raised this evening. Although a specific date has not been fixed by the steering committee, this is a matter which is receiving active attention and I do not think it will be too long before we can come to some agreement as to when an appropriate occasion will present itself.
On the question of auditing procedures which presently govern Air Canada's operation it is true that the Auditor General is not generally involved, simply because the present statutory requirements do not put the Auditor General or Air Canada in that position. The books of Air Canada are, of course, officially audited every year by a firm of chartered accountants, and that auditors' report is carried in every annual report of the airline as a matter of public record, so the House and the country can be well assured that the financial operations of the airline are subject to auditing procedures.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, with reference to the question put earlier today by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) to the minister with respect to certain problems in connection with travel agency matters, the minister indicated that he is following the question very closely and that if there is anything to report to the hon. member or to the House he will be doing so at the very first opportunity.
